On a symmetric family, a finite-horizon lower bound for the average iterate matches the worst-case factor $p^{-1}+ν^{-3}$ up to universal constants. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted scaling.

Systems and Control.title: Scenario-aware Adaptive Neuromorphic Intelligence for multimodal sensor fusion
Systems and Control.summary: Multisensory Physical AI systems operating in isolated conditions must make timely and reliable decisions within strict energy and hardware budgets. In this context, the present analytical study investigates the feasibility of reliable multimodal sensor fusion using a neuromorphic approach based on memristor-based Integrate-and-Fire neuron circuits driven by aggressively compressed representations of sensory information. Rather than relying on fixed processing and learning parameters, the proposed framework introduces scenario-dependent adaptability into individual stages of the neuromorphic decision-making pipeline, including sensor-data compression, nonlinear spike encoding, reliability assessment, and memristive learning-forgetting dynamics. By coupling multiple sensor inputs through adaptive memristive synapses, the framework investigates how reliable and correlated observations can strengthen learned associations, while weak or obsolete relationships gradually decay through nonlinear forgetting. The resulting neuronal responses are evaluated across ten representative driving scenarios derived from the NuScenes dataset by comparing their encoded output patterns with predefined synthetic ground-truth codes representing the expected actuator responses. The simulations demonstrate that scenario-adaptive activity-vector sizing achieves a 61.5% reduction in retained sensory information, while improving mean bit-wise agreement from approximately 55% to 61.2% compared with a fixed maximum-resolution configuration. These findings highlight the potential of introducing scenario-aware adaptability directly into the building blocks of a neuromorphic system, providing a foundation for future hardware implementations that could significantly transform the capabilities of Physical AI systems operating under stringent resource and environmental constraints.

Systems and Control.title: Power-Swing Blocking Scheme Based on Continuous and Higher-Order Incremental Quantities for Systems with Inverter-Based Resources
Systems and Control.summary: Conventional power-swing blocking (PSB) schemes for distance protection face new and emerging challenges as the penetration levels of inverter-based resources (IBRs) increase. Several papers highlight interoperability issues concerning faster power swings and unconventional impedance trajectories. Revised relay settings are proposed in attempts to deal with the problems. However, the blinder-based PSB methodology suffers from being dependent on the speed of the apparent impedance trajectory over the tiny region between the blinders, making it difficult to distinguish between fast swings and faults. Moreover, blinders have the inherent limitation that they cannot operate if the measured impedance is inside the blinders when the fault is cleared and immediately enters the distance zones during the first swing cycle - an issue often overlooked in the current literature. This paper proposes a novel PSB scheme based on higher-order incremental quantities (IQs) for difficult swing scenarios with IBRs and synchronous generators (SGs). PSCAD/EMTDC simulations of an SG and an implemented grid-forming (GFM) inverter validate its superior performance compared to conventional dual-blinder PSB schemes. The impacts of GFM inverters on the impedance measured by distance relays during the fault-to-swing transition and first power swing cycle are also discussed.

Systems and Control.title: Geometry-Evolving Barrier Functions for Safety Evaluation in Dynamic Environments
Systems and Control.summary: Autonomous systems operating in dynamic environments often involve multiple interacting agents, giving rise to high-dimensional safety evaluation problems. Hamilton--Jacobi (HJ) reachability provides rigorous finite-horizon safety guarantees, but solving a global HJ partial differential equation (PDE) over the entire state space leads to prohibitive computational complexity. In this paper, we introduce Geometry-Evolving Barrier Functions (GEBFs), a novel representation for dynamic safety evaluation that propagates local safety geometry of the solution to a terminal-value HJ PDE. By evolving the value, gradient, and curvature information along a Hamiltonian-induced reference trajectory, GEBFs provide a compact representation of the local HJ safety landscape. Under suitable local regularity assumptions, we establish consistency between the GEBF and the value, gradient, and Hessian of the HJ solution along an HJ-optimal characteristic. Building on these theoretical results, we develop an iterative algorithm that couples local geometric propagation with trajectory refinement. We further establish a trajectory-wise one-sided relationship between the GEBF and HJ value function, together with a fixed-point consistency result for the iterative scheme. Experiments on widely adopted agent--obstacle collision-avoidance benchmarks, across low- and high-dimensional systems, demonstrate that GEBFs accurately capture the evolution of dynamic safety boundaries, while achieving substantially lower computational cost than conventional HJ reachability.

Systems and Control.title: EnergyBench: a live, gate-aligned benchmark of day-ahead forecasts for European power markets
Systems and Control.summary: Energy forecasting models are usually compared on backtests and fixed public datasets. Backtests can use data that did not yet exist when the forecast would have been made, and a fixed test set, reused across studies and possibly contained in the pretraining data of foundation models, invites overfitting to the benchmark. EnergyBench evaluates every entry live instead. Each day at 11:30 CET/CEST, thirty minutes before the day-ahead (SDAC) gate closes, every model forecasts the next day's price, wind and solar generation and load on the 15-minute grid for six bidding zones (BE, NL, FR, DE-LU, DK1, DK2). Unlike existing live benchmarks, EnergyBench runs the models itself, on one information set that it freezes at the cut-off and publishes, including three numerical weather prediction models, so that foundation models can be compared with and without the same weather covariates under the actual market deadline. Errors are pooled per series against a seasonal-naive baseline, and models are ranked by a Bradley-Terry rating on the Elo scale with a day-bootstrap interval. The field spans baselines, linear and gradient-boosted models on the frozen weather, eighteen time-series foundation models from eleven families, ensembles, and the grid operators' own forecasts. Over the first thirty-two live days, the covariates reduced the error of each of the ten foundation models run with and without them by 37-51% on matched races (64-73% on wind, 48-61% on solar). Used zero-shot, these models match or outperform a LightGBM model trained on the same covariates. Model size, from 3M to 331M parameters, has a much smaller effect, and median ensembles of the covariate models rank highest. The grid operators' pre-gate forecasts remain ahead on wind and solar, where the best single foundation models have 16-22% more error; on load the gap is 4-6%, within the intervals.
Systems and Control.comment: 21 pages, 10 figures, 7 tables. Live benchmark at https://energybench.foretec.co

Systems and Control.title: Online Optimization for Controlling HVAC Systems
Systems and Control.summary: Heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems account for a significant portion of buildings' energy consumption, motivating the design of energy- and cost-efficient control strategies. However, conventional strategies employ simple, reactive control, without incorporating a model. Therefore, in this paper we adopt an economic model predictive control framework and focus on designing online algorithms to solve the control input design problems with a limited computational budget. In particular, we propose two tailored online algorithms based on projected gradient descent, with a custom projection routine, and the projected primal-dual method. We discuss the pros and cons of both algorithm designs, focusing in particular on computational efficiency. We further compare them through numerical experiments simulating the control of an HVAC system over the course of a day. The results show that computationally efficient online solvers for HVAC systems control are indeed possible. Moreover, the performance closely matches that of a baseline algorithm with unlimited computational budget, in terms of reference temperature tracking and comfort temperature range enforcement.

Systems and Control.title: Generalized Frequency-Domain Stability Analysis Formulation for Multi-Terminal HVDC Systems
Systems and Control.summary: The integration of offshore wind farms (OWFs) and the interconnection of different transmission networks are key drivers for multi-terminal DC (MTDC) systems. Bipolar high-voltage direct current (HVDC) employing dedicated metallic return (DMR) are attractive due to their increased availability, which co-exist with monopolar and rigid bipole configurations. While existing works focus on symmetric operation and particular configurations, we present a unified framework for MTDC stability analysis valid for both symmetric and asymmetric conditions. The formulation uses the minimum number of variables without loss of information, and combines the analytical network representation with black-box converter models, thereby enabling sensitivity studies. In addition, a closed-form expression guiding the stability improvement is presented, which requires minimal data exchange between involved parties. The framework is demonstrated on several case studies of increasing complexity, which highlight the importance of considering intra-station converter couplings and possible uncertainty of network parameters.
Systems and Control.comment: Under review (10 pages). For the associated packages visit http://github.com/Electa-Git/PowerImpedance.jl and http://github.com/Electa-Git/Z-tool

Systems and Control.title: Data-driven current control of modular multilevel converter-based HVDC transmission system
Systems and Control.summary: Model-based design (MBD) is a mature framework for designing the current controllers of modular multilevel converters (MMCs) in high-voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission systems. In MBD, linear state-space models are preferred for their good trade-off between accurate dynamics prediction and simplicity. However, first-principle derivations often neglect relevant MMC dynamics, which can hinder controller performance. Data-driven (DD) methods can deliver less biased models that capture parameter uncertainties, control-loop interactions, and grid dynamics, yet they remain under-exploited for controlling MMC currents. This paper studies DD current control method based on integral Subspace Predictive Control (iSPC), synthesized directly from input--output data measured in a high fidelity real-time digital simulator (RTDS), and proposes an initial guideline outlining the main steps for its systematic application to MMC current control. The proposed iSPC is compared against state-of-the-art DD solution, and the findings are validated through simulation studies in MATLAB/Simulink.
Systems and Control.comment: 8 pages, submitted to IET AC and DC Power Transmission (ACDC)

Systems and Control.title: To Learn or Not to Learn: A Screening Test for Control Problems Before Reinforcement Learning
Systems and Control.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) can be a powerful alternative to classical control methods when standard model-based control is insufficient, e.g., when deriving a suitable model is intractable or impossible. However, in many cases, the choice between model-based and RL-based control is not obvious. Because training RL agents is computationally expensive, RL should be limited to cases where it is expected to outperform model-based control. To the best of our knowledge, there exists no approach to automatically screen out control problems before RL training for which RL is not expected to yield any benefit. In this work, we take the first step towards such an automated screening test. We present a test that identifies problems for which RL-based control is not expected to be superior in two steps. Only control problems that pass both steps should be considered for RL. Part I evaluates the suitability of a provided model for model-based control by analyzing the impact of its uncertainties on the control problem. For this, we use reachset-conformant system identification combined with simulation-based analysis. If the uncertainties are found to be relevant in Part I, Part II then evaluates their learnability using a statistically calibrated dependence analysis. We apply our screening test to several benchmarks, reliably identifying control problems for which RL-based control does not measurably improve upon model-based control, thereby achieving a speed-up of up to $21\times$ compared to trying RL.
Systems and Control.comment: This work is currently under review

Systems and Control.title: Towards Track Height Control in Additive Manufacturing on Porous Substrates: An Approach for System Identification and Controller Selection
Systems and Control.summary: Additive manufacturing is transforming the creation of materials and parts, enabling the design and manufacturing of multifunctional parts with tailored properties. One compelling example is the combination of a porous core and a non-porous surface, which offers significant advantages in terms of weight reduction, material efficiency, strength and wear resistance. Directed Energy Deposition (DED) processes enable the transition from porous core to non-porous part surface by closing the pores. However, the surface-layer of porous substrates presents a substantial challenge to achieving consistent track heights during DED, directly impacting the final part geometry and performance. Therefore, precise control of the deposition process is crucial for realising the full potential of the multifunctional parts. In order to address this challenge, this work presents a conceptual approach for track height control during Laser-based Directed Energy Deposition (DED-LB) on porous substrates. First, the DED-LB process and the associated measurement setup are explained, along with a discussion of their limitations. The focus then shifts to the control problem, beginning with system identification to characterise the process dynamics. Subsequently, a selection of control strategies is investigated, as well as their compatibility with the process. This research provides a foundational step toward reliable additive manufacturing on porous substrates, and thus toward producing multifunctional parts.

Systems and Control.title: K-subareas partitioning subject to coinciding boundary segments of neighboring subareas
Systems and Control.summary: A method for the problem of partitioning an area into K subareas subject to coinciding boundary segments of neighboring subareas is presented. The given area may be non-convex and may additionally include obstacle areas. The proposed hierarchical method involves three steps: repeated bisection splitting, merging and the solution of traveling salesman problems. Geographic real-world outdoors areas data is used for the evaluation of the method. The benefit of computational simplicity at the cost of imbalanced subarea sizes is highlighted.

Systems and Control.title: A Cost-Effective Submodule with Fault-Blocking Capability for Modular Multilevel Converters
Systems and Control.summary: Modular multilevel converter (MMC) has become an attractive technology for high-power electronics applications thanks to its high energy efficiency, high power rating, high modularity, flexible scalability, and superior output waveform quality. It has attracted considerable research attention, and numerous submodule (SM) variants have been developed for different objectives. Among them, the half-bridge SM (HBSM) is the most widely adopted thanks to its simplicity, but it cannot interrupt DC-side short-circuit currents. Various SM topologies with fault-blocking capability have been proposed. These SM topologies contain additional switches and passive components compared to the HBSM, leading to higher capital and operating costs. Aiming at these issue, an SM topology capable to block DC-side fault-currents with a reduced component count is proposed in this paper. The proposed SM includes two variants, one employs only two fully-controlled switches. An operation and control scheme for the proposed SM are also developed and presented in the paper. The functionality of the proposed SM is validated by experiment, and the value of the SM is demonstrated through a test simulation for an high-voltage direct-current (HVDC) transmission system.

Systems and Control.title: A Conformal Transmit-Reflect Array Enabling Multifunctional Bidirectional Beam Switching for Emergency Communication System
Systems and Control.summary: This article presents a conformal transmit-reflect array (CTRA) that enables bidirectional multibeam switching through a single metasurface aperture for emergency communication applications. To realize reconfigurable bidirectional beam switching, a transmit-reflect integrated element (TRIE) is developed by combining a polarization-selective transmissive structure with a complementary-symmetric reflective structure. The proposed element enables independent control of the cross-polarized transmission and reflection phases while exhibiting stable performance under oblique incidence. To support practical conformal implementations, a geometrical-optics-based phase compensation method is applied to cylindrical geometries, enabling effective wavefront control across the conformal aperture. By incorporating a polarization-switchable feed array (PSFA), multifunctional beam switching is achieved in the forward, backward, and bidirectional operating modes. The PSFA is configured as a nonuniform curved linear array near the focal region, enabling feed-selective beam switching within $\pm 30^\circ$ in both the $+z$ and $-z$ directions through selective excitation of the corresponding feed elements. The full-wave simulation results agree well with the measurements. The proposed CTRA achieves peak gains of 24.1 and 24.8 dBi in the forward and backward modes, respectively. The maximum aperture efficiencies in the forward and backward operating states are 28.4$\%$ and 33.4$\%$. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and flexibility of the proposed CTRA, making it a promising candidate for adaptive emergency communication systems.

Systems and Control.title: Learning and Steering in Incomplete-Information Games
Systems and Control.summary: In many modern multi-agent systems, a mediator seeks to influence strategic decision dynamics using only outcome-level feedback and without knowing agents' utilities. In this work, we study how a mediator can learn an unknown game and steer adaptive agents toward outcomes that maximize her utility using only trajectory feedback. The mediator knows the game form and her own objective, but not the agents' utilities. Moreover, she commits to nonnegative payments and provides recommendations and contexts, but receives only a single realized terminal outcome rather than full-information feedback. We develop halving-type algorithms that learn utility differences in normal-form games and conditional continuation-value differences in extensive-form games, achieving a sample complexity of $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ that matches worst-case lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. We then combine these learning procedures with a Lagrangian formulation in an online Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm that interleaves learning, equilibrium computation, and steering toward mediator-optimal extensive-form correlated equilibria (EFCE). With high probability, the Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm achieves a directness gap and an optimality gap of $\widetilde O(T^{-1/4})$, while time-average payments are of $\widetilde O(T^{-1/8})$.

Systems and Control.title: Modeling Rainwater Harvesting Systems with Covered Storage Tank on A Smartphone
Systems and Control.summary: A model for simulating rainwater harvesting systems with a covered storage tank is described. The model is simple enough to serve as the simulation engine of a smartphone app for designing such systems. The results of the simulation can be used to find the optimum tank size and the reliability of the system in meeting a given demand. This is illustrated by using the model for designing two such systems, one in an urban environment and the other in an arid rural location. The Python scripts used for the simulations are included as ancillary material.
Systems and Control.comment: Version 2: revised and extended analysis; 21 pages, 13 figures. Python translation of the model, scripts and ERA5 data provided as ancillary files

Systems and Control.title: dynamicalnodes: Block Diagrams to ROS2 Graphs
Systems and Control.summary: Here we introduce dynamicalnodes, a framework for rapid iterative prototyping of control and estimation algorithms within the Robot Operating System, or ROS. The framework leverages the theory of discrete-time dynamical systems to encode each component of a feedback system (e.g. reference generator, controller, plant, observer) as a pair of functions, denoted $(f,\,h) $, where $f$ is an evolution function and $h$ is an output function. With appropriate choice of domain and codomain, the $ (f,\,h) $ pairs can be composed to form feedback systems of arbitrary complexity. Moving from theory to practice, the user implements each $(f,\,h)$ pair in Python and encapsulates them in objects that facilitate composition and simulation. ROS executables are generated from these objects via rclpy, where relevant metadata such as network topology and publishing frequency are written automatically. The final result is a collection of rclpy files from which validated feedback systems can be spun up as live ROS graphs. We discuss the relevant theory behind the framework and then demonstrate the prototyping workflow applied to a canonical controls problem, a car with cruise control.

Systems and Control.title: Single-stage joint diffusion of sky images and clear-sky index for ultra-short-term irradiance forecasting: what the frame-to-irradiance stage discards
Systems and Control.summary: Sky-image irradiance forecasting is dominated by a two-stage design: a video-prediction model forecasts future sky frames, and a separately trained regressor maps those frames to irradiance. We propose a single-stage alternative that co-denoises the future sky-image and clear-sky-index sequences in one diffusion process, with an irradiance head that reads a denoised preview of the future sky rather than the noised diffusion state. The forecaster needs no regression stage and runs from sky images and deterministic covariates alone, with no measured irradiance at its input --- the situation at a site with a camera but no pyranometer. On 2023 SIRTA data the model reaches a pooled RMSE of $104.1$~W\,m$^{-2}$ and a skill score of $+0.34$ on the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) against smart persistence, higher than any of twelve baseline configurations, and retains that skill when retrained on 2021--2022. On the model's own generated frames, a separately trained regressor reaches $150.6$~W\,m$^{-2}$ against the joint head's $104.1$: roughly $46$~W\,m$^{-2}$ that joint training recovers and a cascade discards. Point accuracy is competitive but not best: a deterministic network that also reads measured irradiance attains $97.6$~W\,m$^{-2}$. The model's CRPS skill leads that network's in every sky-condition tertile, by $0.26$ to $0.30$.

Systems and Control.title: Unified Overview of Safety Certificate Functions: Techniques from Hamilton--Jacobi Reachability and Control Barrier Functions
Systems and Control.summary: Safety is a central concern in modern autonomous systems. Safety certificates---functions whose existence guarantees that a system meets its safety specification---have long been used as a principled tool for rigorously reasoning about safety. Methods for synthesizing such certificates are scattered across research areas, with little guidance on when to use a particular approach. This tutorial provides a holistic treatment of safety certificate synthesis centered on two widely used families: Hamilton--Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis and control barrier functions (CBFs). For each family of methods, we first introduce its general formulation, along with classical and learning-based tools for certificate synthesis. Next, we introduce two benchmark problems consisting of vehicle systems of differing complexity to assess the certificate quality of different synthesis methods and their effectiveness in safety-critical control. We use these benchmarks to compare various methods and provide practical guidance for selecting an approach.

Systems and Control.title: Training-Independent Validation of a Learning-Based Controller for Stunt Maneuvers
Systems and Control.summary: Learned controllers for vehicle maneuvers are usually validated under the conditions and objective used to train them, where they appear highly reliable, yet the parameters that change on real roads are often not those the model was trained on. We argue that validation must be independent of training: it should vary physical parameters that training kept fixed and use acceptance criteria absent from the training objective. A learning-based control policy, G-Maneuver, with 90.11% success is tested for stunt-level maneuvers. A looser terminal-heading score ranked the worst setting as the best. Because real stunt tests are safety-critical, a simulation-to-reality-to-simulation (Sim2Real2Sim) loop uses the simulation to select safe zones for real-vehicle trials with 16.9% acceptance. Automotive safety analysis frameworks are used to identify parameters for validation using coverage tests. We demonstrated that the kinematic stunt-driving indicators, namely heading change, sideslip, and speed-normalized yaw rate, match between simulation and the real world, while force and roll indicators do not, which identifies the indicators that can support safe deployment. A video of the experiments is available at https://youtu.be/dN1Oes8pNIo.

Systems and Control.title: Simulation Modeling and Control of an Elastic Shaping Antagonistic Variable Stiffness Actuator
Systems and Control.summary: Position--stiffness regulation of antagonistic variable stiffness actuators (VSAs) involves coupled nonlinear dynamics, parameter uncertainty, and feedback states that are not directly measured. This paper addresses this challenge through a simulation-based workflow that integrates elastic shaping, model verification, and layered nonlinear control. This study builds on a previously developed actuator comprising two crossed four-bar compliant transmission elastic units. Its optimized elastic mapping provides the structural basis, with an ADAMS torque-curve root mean square error (RMSE) of $2.57\,\mathrm{N\!\cdot\!mm}$ against the target. A control-oriented analytical model is implemented in Simulink and compared with the independently executed ADAMS model under matched inputs. The maximum joint-angle RMSE across the tested cases is $4.66\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{rad}$. A layered controller combines extended Kalman filtering for state reconstruction, feedback linearization for nominal decoupling, and adaptive sliding-mode control for residual compensation. At the end of the nominal simulation, the joint-angle error is approximately $3.14\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{rad}$. The stiffness error is $3.07\,\mathrm{N\!\cdot\!mm/rad}$ relative to a target of $50\,\mathrm{N\!\cdot\!mm/rad}$. Parameter-variation and ablation tests assess tracking performance and the effects of the controller modules within the evaluated conditions. The resulting workflow links structural-response modeling, state estimation, and robust control assessment, supporting repeatable comparisons beyond nominal tracking alone.
Systems and Control.comment: 29 pages, 11 figures. Extends the structural study in arXiv:2609.18456 (ACIRS 2026) with dynamic modeling and closed-loop control evaluation

Systems and Control.title: Kinematic analysis of a double-closed-loop four-bar chain-based leg for a multimodal quadruped-pentarotor robot
Systems and Control.summary: This paper presents the kinematic modeling and singularity analysis of a three-degree-of-freedom, double four-bar closed-loop quadruped leg mechanism. This leg is essential for transitioning between the two operational modes; therefore, it is examined in both joint and task spaces, leading to the development of its Jacobian matrix, which is vital for designing the gaits required for terrestrial mode and mid-air aerial reconfiguration (for aerial mode). Various gaits are devised for the system's motion in the MATLAB simulation, and their practical implementation on the single-leg test rig is demonstrated.
Systems and Control.comment: Journal paper submitted to Robotica with ID:ROB-2026-0373

Systems and Control.title: ZipDrift: Generating Multimodal Short-Horizon MPC Costs with One-Step Drifting Models
Systems and Control.summary: Short-horizon model predictive control (MPC) is fast but myopic. ZipMPC compensates by learning a context-dependent correction of the short-horizon cost that imitates a long-horizon expert. We observe that the optimal correction is often multimodal: when a slower opponent can be passed on either side, good corrections of opposite sign coexist, and the expert's choice between them hinges on tiny cost differences. Deterministic regression then averages modes or inherits inconsistent expert tie-breaking. We propose ZipDrift, which trains a one-step drifting generator over MPC cost corrections, tilted toward low closed-loop cost and learned only from cost evaluations of candidate corrections, without differentiating through the optimiser. A few generated candidates are ranked by a learned critic, and the model-based MPC then enforces dynamics and constraints. In a kinematic overtaking benchmark derived from ZipMPC, more than half of the contexts are bimodal and the manual short-horizon MPC crashes in 28% of them. With an eight-dimensional stagewise correction, evaluated on 1000 fresh contexts and five training seeds, ZipDrift with eight candidates crashes in 0.74% of episodes, compared with 3.4% for an idealised ZipMPC-style regressor and 2.1% for critic-ranked random candidates with the same budget. A mixture density network (MDN) with the same selection is equally good (0.76%). The benefit of drifting lies in sample quality: in a pre-specified test on further unseen contexts, a single drifting sample crashes in 8.7% of episodes against 13.2% for the MDN, and ZipDrift needs four candidates instead of eight to fall below 1%. With many candidates, all methods degrade as selection exploits errors of the critic.
Systems and Control.comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Preliminary simulation study

Systems and Control.title: Two-stage residual learning for calibrated uncertainty in solar irradiance forecasts
Systems and Control.summary: Accurate forecasting of renewable generation requires not only point predictions but also reliable estimates of the uncertainty attached to them, particularly at extended horizons. Machine learning models are increasingly used to predict solar output, but they typically report a single value and capture the associated uncertainty poorly. The standard remedy is to train a model to predict the parameters of an assumed probability distribution directly. Here we develop an alternative two-stage method, motivated by synthetic solar signal generation, in which the forecast error is modeled separately from the expected irradiance. A first long short-term memory (LSTM) network predicts the expected global horizontal irradiance, and a second network models the distribution of the forecast error, which is added back to the mean to give both the forecast and its uncertainty. Using historical weather data from the National Solar Radiation Database and a probability integral transform evaluation, we show that explicitly modeling the error brings the predicted standard deviation markedly closer to the historical value, reducing the deviation between the two by 34.6 percent for a standalone LSTM and by 56.5 percent when the LSTM is coupled to Gaussian process regression, the most reliable of the configurations tested. Because the method models the total forecast error directly, it captures the full predictive uncertainty that matters for decisions, rather than only the model contribution that dropout-based approaches estimate.

Systems and Control.title: Safe Output-Regulation Flows for Constrained Optimization via Control Barrier Functions
Systems and Control.summary: Control-theoretic approaches to constrained optimization have been widely studied by interpreting optimization algorithms as dynamical systems. This paper formulates constrained optimization as an output-regulation problem with state constraints, where equality-constraint residuals are treated as regulated outputs and inequality constraints as state constraints. Proportional--integral feedback is employed to drive the equality-constraint residuals asymptotically to zero, while a control barrier function (CBF) safety filter is used to ensure inequality safety throughout the optimization process. We establish feasibility of the CBF filtering program throughout the inequality-feasible set and local exponential convergence of the resulting flow. Under stronger global conditions, we further prove convergence from an entire connected component of the inequality-feasible set. Since exact implementation of the flow requires solving a CBF quadratic program at each state, we further develop a flow that approximates the CBF solution through multiplier updates. Moreover, we provide a unified formulation encompassing the two proposed flows and projected primal--dual dynamics. Numerical examples demonstrate convergence, safety, and computational tradeoffs of the proposed flows.

Systems and Control.title: Truncated backpropagation through time induces a two-sided gradient turnpike property
Systems and Control.summary: Truncated backpropagation through time reduces the computational burden of training recurrent models by restricting gradient computations to shorter temporal contexts. This induces two distinct boundary effects: missing past information perturbs the forward state evolution, while truncating the backward recursion omits future information. This motivates decoupling the interval over which gradient contributions are averaged for the parameter update from the surrounding temporal context over which they are computed. Under exponential decay of the state-transition Jacobians and mild regularity conditions, this leads to a two-sided gradient turnpike property: the error between truncated- and full-context gradient contributions decays exponentially with the distance from both context boundaries. We derive bounds for the averaged update gradient, yielding guarantees on gradient alignment and approximate full-context stationarity; under unbiased interval sampling and a Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition, these further imply a bound on the resulting optimality gap. Numerical experiments on the Wiener-Hammerstein benchmark illustrate the role of past and future context and the trade-off between predictive performance and computational cost.

Systems and Control.title: A Novel Asymmetric Distributed Voltage Regulation Scheme to Enhance the Utilization of Distributed Energy Resources
Systems and Control.summary: Passive voltage regulation in distribution grids using distributed energy resources (DERs) is becoming the standard for feeder voltage management in both under-voltage and over-voltage scenarios. Their simple control, ease of implementation, and fast response make them ideal for distribution feeders with high-DER penetration. This paper proposes a novel distributed voltage control for DERs based on the voltage at the point of common coupling, inverter rating, and operating active power. The proposed control is designed to utilize feeder inverters efficiently to reduce the burden on the inverters in both under-voltage and over-voltage operations and increase the fairness in reactive power ($Q$) support in over-voltage operations. The proposed control is implemented in static and dynamic simulations of a real feeder to validate the performance. Results for the under-voltage scenario are also presented in the paper.

Systems and Control.title: Dynamic Watermarking and Action-Conditioned Latent Dynamics for Secure Vision-Based Controllers
Systems and Control.summary: Replay attacks are difficult to detect in vision-based control systems because previously recorded observations can remain plausible while the physical system follows a different trajectory. This paper develops an adaptive dynamic-watermarking framework for detecting replay attacks against vision-based controllers. A private Gaussian watermark is added to the nominal control input, and a control input-conditioned latent dynamics network (LDN) predicts the corresponding evolution in a compact latent space learned from image observations. Attack evidence is obtained from the discrepancy between the predicted latent response and the latent representation of the received image observation. A reinforcement learning policy adjusts the watermark covariance using the latent state and detector confidence, thereby balancing attack detectability, watermark energy, and control distortion. A Lagrangian penalty on task-specific safety costs is included during training to limit the adverse effect of the excitation. The framework is evaluated on a vision-guided UR5 manipulation task in which the robot reaches a target while avoiding a moving human arm under nominal and replay-attacked observations.
Systems and Control.comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, Submitted to ACC 2027 conference

Systems and Control.title: Distributed Robust Model Predictive Control for Optimal Consensus of Unknown Multiagent Systems with Event-Triggered Communication
Systems and Control.summary: In this paper, we study the optimal consensus problem for multiagent systems with unknown dynamics. We propose a robust model predictive control (MPC) framework that jointly optimizes the control input and consensus sequences while enforcing state and input constraints. Within this framework, noisy offline data are used to construct nominal prediction models and quantify the associated uncertainty, which is explicitly incorporated into the robust MPC design. To solve the resulting optimization problem at each MPC update with reduced inter-agent communication, we develop a distributed gradient-projection alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm with an event-triggered information exchange mechanism and establish its convergence to the optimal solution. Furthermore, sufficient conditions are established to guarantee robust constraint satisfaction and practical consensus of the closed-loop multiagent system. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

Systems and Control.title: ThermoLLM: LLM-Based Multi-Zone HVAC Control with a Spatiotemporal Context
Systems and Control.summary: Multi-zone HVAC control is a spatial decision problem in which indoor thermal evolution and control decisions depend not only on outdoor conditions and internal heat gains but also on zone layout, physical adjacency, and delayed thermal interactions across the building. Recent LLM-based HVAC controllers have shown that prompt-based control is feasible. However, these methods produce inconsistent results, are difficult to generalize, and experience control-latency issues. Their performance also relies heavily on numeric reward values, textual feedback, or unstructured retrieval, which limits their ability to make control decisions that account for zone dynamics and thermodynamics. No existing LLM-based methods have used building semantics and dynamics, together with rolling history, as the centre of the LLM context while testing and comparing HVAC control performance with existing LLM-based HVAC approaches. This paper presents ThermoLLM, an LLM-based HVAC control framework tested in a multi-zone building environment. Spatiotemporal context grounding is a main component of ThermoLLM, which uses a spatial knowledge graph derived from Brick-style building semantics and linked with recent observations from a rolling history. We evaluate ThermoLLM against standard control methods and recent state-of-the-art baselines in a five-zone building environment across six climate-season scenarios. ThermoLLM consistently achieves the best energy-comfort trade-offs and outperforms all evaluated baselines in the Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS) rankings across all six scenarios.

Systems and Control.title: A Synchronized Tri-Modality Wireless System for Multi-Point Non-Contact Cardiac Monitoring
Systems and Control.summary: Cardiac physiological monitoring is fundamental to evaluating cardiovascular health and diagnosing related diseases. Non-contact radar sensing can capture chest-wall vibrations with spatial specificity, enabling localized physiological monitoring and cardiac assessment. Progress, however, has been limited by the absence of a reliable, research-grade hardware platform for rigorous validation of radar-based methods. Prior systems typically pair radar, namely Doppler cardiography (DCG), with only electrocardiography (ECG) or other coarse references, providing no direct mechanical ground truth and thus constraining fine-grained evaluation of radar outputs. We present a tri-modality wireless system that integrates ECG, seismocardiography (SCG), and DCG under a unified acquisition and control framework for time-aligned recording and analysis. The tri-modality system combines miniaturized wearable ECG/SCG modules with a high-resolution mmWave radar module, supporting spatially resolved sensing and subsequent feature extraction. To our knowledge, this is the first integrated ECG--SCG--DCG hardware system for comprehensive cardiac monitoring; it enables multi-point thoracic acquisition, achieves precise cross-modal synchronization, and maintains specifications suitable for wearable operation. Experiments on a linear-motion platform show close agreement between DCG- and SCG-derived displacements, confirming accurate displacement measurement. Human-subject studies further demonstrate cross-modal consistency and robust extraction of feature points, establishing ECG as the electrical anchor and SCG as the mechanical ground truth for DCG. Overall, the system provides a rigorous, spatially resolved validation platform that advances non-contact cardiac sensing and supports next-generation radar-based monitoring.

Systems and Control.title: A Framework for Guaranteed Active Fault Diagnosis with Applications to Aircraft Systems
Systems and Control.summary: Within the multiple-model framework, active fault diagnosis applies auxiliary control input signals to ex?cite the system such that fault modes are distinguishable. For aircraft systems, it has been pointed out by some rele?vant works that certain faults cannot be effectively detected and isolated in time without actively exciting the aircraft dynamics. However, existing works have not simultane?ously addressed the optimal auxiliary control design with theoretical guarantees and the FDI method with an effective mechanism for triggering the active fault diagnosis. Hence, we are motivated to propose a framework of active FDI for aircraft systems to explicitly address the aforementioned issue. Specifically, we first formulate a receding-horizon FDI scheme for estimating the likelihood of candidate fault modes with proved effectiveness, and then we propose a method for estimating mode probabilities, based on which a mechanism is designed for triggering auxiliary control for active fault diagnosis. The auxiliary control signal design is formulated such that the effectiveness for FDI is theoret?ically guaranteed and the disruption to nominal flight oper?ation is minimized. Numerical test results are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

Systems and Control.title: An Ordering Optimization for Fruit-Vegetable in High-Density Environment based on Genetic Algorithm
Systems and Control.summary: This paper presents a robotic harvesting method that combines RGB-D fruit localization, GA-based harvest ordering, and waypoint-based robot motion in dense and unstructured crop environments. The global RGB-D camera provides 3D fruit positions for ordering, while the end-effector-mounted camera provides close-range observation during execution. The GA determines the harvesting sequence, and static or dynamic waypoints define the intermediate robot motion. The method was evaluated in a controlled laboratory testbed and in four-, five-, and six-fruit field conditions. GA solutions were compared with exhaustive enumeration, and both waypoint offsets were examined by parameter sensitivity analysis. Continuous execution reduced unnecessary Home-return motion, while the dynamic waypoint changed with the remaining fruit distribution without changing the GA sequence. In the field evaluation, the dynamic-waypoint continuous strategy produced 40 collision events and a 70.7% target-approach success rate, compared with 55 collision events and 65.3% for the static-waypoint continuous strategy.

Systems and Control.title: How do Transformers Perform Low-Level Control In-Context?
Systems and Control.summary: One of the remarkable abilities of Transformer-based neural networks is in-context learning. This motivates us to think about "in-context" control. Can we control a system knowing only (1) that it belongs to a particular family of systems and (2) some data on system evolution (provided as the context trajectory) but no specific parameter information? Specifically, we investigate the ability of Transformer-models to perform "in-context" control of unstable, nonlinear dynamical systems, where context consists only of the unforced system dynamics. We leverage a multi-head, GPT-2-style architecture, and we evaluate performance for two classical nonlinear systems -- the cartpole system and the two-link acrobot system, where the system parameters are unknown to the Transformer. We consider a setting where trajectories from an expert controller are available at training time but not at inference time. Here, we identify training techniques that are essential to train Transformers to perform low-level control. Through an analysis over checkpoints, we show that in-context control is possible, and the learned policy performance generally improves as context increases. Furthermore, the Transformer models can generalize to stabilize systems that are out-of-distribution.
Systems and Control.comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, Accepted to the 65th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC 2026)

Systems and Control.title: State-Feedback Passivity Control for Synchronous Machine Systems
Systems and Control.summary: The passivity of a generating station enables network stability to be established from conditions verified locally at each station. For synchronous machines, however, passivity can only be certified under conditions on the operating point, and these conditions fail under heavy loading and weak damping. This paper develops a state-feedback controller that enforces passivity using a storage battery connected at the terminal bus. A bilinear term arising from the product of the rotor-speed and stator-current deviations is treated as a bounded uncertainty, leading to robust positive-real conditions that can be enforced by a state feedback control designed using a single algebraic Riccati equation. The resulting controller guarantees passivity whenever the Riccati equation admits a positive-definite solution, with no separate condition on the operating point. Numerical examples show that existing conditions certify passivity only up to a fraction of the rated current, whereas the proposed state-feedback approach certifies it at the rated operating point of the machine.

Systems and Control.title: Worst-Case Discovery and Runtime Protection for RL-Based Network Controllers
Systems and Control.summary:
RL-based controllers achieve strong average-case performance in networking tasks such as congestion control and adaptive bitrate streaming. Yet their performance can degrade severely under network conditions where strong performance is still achievable. Identifying such conditions and quantifying the resulting performance gap is intractable by enumeration, while the sequential and closed-loop nature of RL controllers makes formal verification methods impractical.
  We present ReGuard, a framework that discovers worst-case scenarios for a given RL controller and protects it against them at inference time without retraining. ReGuard formulates scenario discovery as a bilevel regret-maximization problem, certifying a lower bound on the controller's worst-case performance gap. ReGuard then analyzes the discovered counterfactual trajectories and compiles them into lightweight logic rules that intervene only when a risky state is detected, leaving the controller's behavior unchanged otherwise.
  We evaluate ReGuard across three RL-based network controllers: Pensieve, Sage, and Park. ReGuard discovers scenarios in which each controller suffers a 43-64% performance loss relative to what is achievable under the same conditions. ReGuard exposes performance gaps 57% to 6 times larger than those found by the strongest baselines and shrinks those gaps by 79-85% in its first iteration via lightweight rule-based protection, iteratively driving the remaining gap toward nominal levels. ReGuard's protection extends beyond the scenarios it discovers, improving performance across a wide range of network conditions.

Systems and Control.title: Tags Helping Tags: Coordination-Free Power Boosting for Battery-less Backscatter Networks
Systems and Control.summary: Battery-less backscatter sensor nodes powered by radio-frequency wireless power transfer are attractive for large or hard-to-reach deployments, but their range is typically limited by the forward power-transfer link rather than by communication sensitivity. We present a method for improving power delivery, and thus range, in dense tag deployments by having nearby tags act as helpers: each helper terminates its antenna in purely reactive impedances, reflecting the power beacon's signal toward a target tag so that it combines constructively with the direct line-of-sight path and increases the power the target harvests. On a hardware testbed, helpers using discrete impedance control are shown to increase the target tag's harvested power by over 50% above an all-absorbing baseline, while randomly set helper impedances give no reliable benefit, and are sometimes even detrimental. We further propose and implement a local algorithm that lets each helper tune its own impedance using only measurements of the target's packet rate, without channel estimation or coordination between helpers, and we show that it brings the target's packet rate close to that of an independently tuned configuration. These results suggest that independent, passive sensor nodes can cooperatively extend each other's power-transfer range with minimal added infrastructure.

Systems and Control.title: Reducing Data-Center Load Transfers with Ride-Through-Aware Voltage Control
Systems and Control.summary: Fault-induced transfers of large data centers to backup supply can cause abrupt reductions in grid-served demand. Coordinating reactive-power support to mitigate these transfers requires consideration of facility-specific voltage--duration ride-through characteristics, particularly when support capacity is limited. This paper develops a ride-through-aware extension of quadratic voltage control that assesses voltage deviations relative to the admissible margins specified by these characteristics. We establish four design requirements that jointly express envelope-based severity, duration dependence, and preventive voltage-restoration incentives. Within a multiplicatively gated quadratic class, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for satisfying these requirements and construct an explicit family of envelope-normalized objectives. We apply the proposed objectives to reactive-power coordination and evaluate their performance on the IEEE 14-bus, New England 39-bus, and NPCC 140-bus systems. Comparisons with Volt/VAR control, conventional nominal-voltage tracking, and recent data-center voltage-control methods demonstrate improved data-center retention under matched reactive-power support constraints. In the IEEE 14-bus study, the proposed controller reduces the mean data-center disconnection rate by 44.8\% and grid-demand loss by 27.4\% compared with the best-performing baseline. These results highlight the benefit of incorporating data-center ride-through requirements into reactive-power allocation.

Systems and Control.title: Robust Adaptive Lyapunov-Based MPC for Nonlinear Systems with Experimental Validation on Quadcopter Attitude Control
Systems and Control.summary: In this paper, a computationally efficient robust adaptive Lyapunov-based model predictive control (RALMPC) framework is proposed for a class of constrained nonlinear systems subject to uncertainties and external disturbances. A radial basis function neural network (RBFNN), introduced to approximate non-parametric uncertainties, is incorporated into a control Lyapunov function analysis, together with integral barrier Lyapunov functionals for state constraint enforcement. This analysis yields control and adaptation laws for parametric uncertainties, external disturbances, RBFNN weights, and worst-case approximation error, rendering the closed-loop system uniformly bounded while ensuring convergence of tracking errors to compact sets around the origin. The resulting guarantees are then embedded into the RALMPC optimal control problem through a contractive constraint, thus combining formal closed-loop stability with real-time performance optimization; at the same time, the adaptation laws allow the RALMPC prediction model to be updated online. Comparative hardware-in-the-loop simulations against state-of-the-art MPC schemes validate the efficacy and computational efficiency of the proposed framework. Ultimately, RALMPC is experimentally validated on a custom-built quadcopter platform for time-varying attitude tracking, demonstrating its practical feasibility; comparisons against alternative strategies confirm its superiority in achieving improved closed-loop performance.

Systems and Control.title: Optical Network Digital Twin -- Practical Use Cases and Architecture
Systems and Control.summary: With the widespread adoption of AI, machine-to-machine communications are rapidly increasing, reshaping the requirements for optical networks. Recent advances in Gaussian noise modeling for digital coherent transmission have raised expectations for digital-twin-based operation. However, unlike digital twins in wireless communication, which are already well established, significant barriers remain for commercialization in optical networks. This paper discusses the evolving requirements of optical networks in the AI era and proposes a practical Optical Network Digital Twin architecture enabling dynamic and Quality of Transmission aware operation beyond conventional management. Representative use cases, including operator-driven optimization, user-operator collaboration, and multi-operator interconnection, are presented, along with the architectural framework and key challenges toward practical deployment.

Systems and Control.title: FishSense Lite: A Camera-Based, Single Laser Hardware Framework with Software System for In Situ Fish Length Measurement
Systems and Control.summary: Fish stock assessments need fish lengths paired with species from far more places than trained surveyors can reach. Recreational divers already visit many of those places, but measuring a fish underwater has required trained observers or specialist equipment. We present FishSense Lite, which recovers fish length from a single photograph taken with a recreational dive camera, a dive laser pointer, and a 3D-printed mount. The diver aims the laser at a fish and takes a picture; afterward, the dot's position in the image gives the range to the fish, and the range turns the fish's size in the image into a length. A citizen-science program, trained by the system's builders, taught its own divers and collected lengths paired with species for 73 wild fish across seven open-water dives. On seven wild fish also measured by an underwater stereo-imaging system, the two instruments agreed without detectable bias (mean difference +0.8%). On rigid targets of known length, FishSense Lite recovered every target to within 1.3%, and 99% of 1,055 frames fell within a 15% error budget. From the error sources we measure, we derive a field protocol: calibrate against a dive slate on every dive, photograph fish within 15 degrees of perpendicular and beyond 1 m, and take at least ten frames of each.

Systems and Control.title: Vector Lyapunov functions for nonconvex constrained optimization
Systems and Control.summary: Nonconvex constrained optimization problems are commonly solved by a Newton method for necessary conditions (sequential linear/quadratic programming) or a barrier reformulation (interior-point methods). We present a vector Lyapunov analysis for Newton-type algorithms based on constraint violation and optimality of the primal solutions to a sequence of approximate optimization problems. We thus prove local stability and convergence by constructing a strict Lyapunov function for the primal solution.
Systems and Control.comment: Extended version of submission to the 2027 European Control Conference

Systems and Control.title: Residential Vehicle-to-Grid Deployment: A United States-Based Stakeholder Perspective
Systems and Control.summary:
The integration of vehicle-to-grid (V2G), in which electric vehicle (EV) owners can send electricity from their vehicles back to the grid, is an emerging solution to enhance grid resilience. However, V2G deployment in the United States lags behind many other countries. This can be attributed to a broad range of factors, and to investigate them, this study analyzes semi-structured interviews with stakeholders using inductive-deductive qualitative coding. Results from the interviews are coded across financial, technical, social, political, and organizational dimensions in order to understand the three main deployment factors of drivers, benefits, and barriers of V2G. Once coded, the relationships between these factors are used to construct a cognitive map to identify actions that will most effectively drive V2G deployment.
  The results indicate that grid resilience and decarbonization are seen as the main benefits of V2G. User willingness to participate, a lack of technological readiness and standardization, prohibitive costs, and unsupportive laws and policies are among the most frequently cited barriers. Connections in the cognitive map indicate that the most closely related drivers for mitigating these barriers are user compensation for battery degradation, community outreach, the creation of grid interconnection standards and protocols, and supportive grants and policy frameworks for V2G piloting and adoption.

Systems and Control.title: A Memory Efficient Unified Algorithm for Online Learning of Linear Dynamical Systems
Systems and Control.summary: Motivated by the challenge of stabilizing a general unknown linear dynamical system (LDS) from observations, we study the natural prerequisite of online prediction. Our goal is to achieve sublinear regret with a memory footprint that adapts to the intrinsic complexity of the dynamics rather than the full hidden-state dimension. We focus on the practically central regime of systems with low instability complexity -- eigenvalues outside the real stable interval that do not decay rapidly, together with non-semisimple modes -- potentially embedded in an otherwise stable real spectrum of much higher dimension; we write $k$ for this count. This regime is the primary setting in which stabilization is plausible: we show that many systems with high instability complexity cannot be stabilized without exponentially large controls. Thus, prediction is meaningful for stabilization precisely when the instability complexity is small. Within this regime, we introduce a unified online algorithm that handles every LDS (including non-diagonalizable systems with complex or exploding modes) with a learnable parameter count of $\widetilde{O}(k)$. Finally, we prove a lower bound showing that $k$ is a valid complexity measure: any filter-based predictor needs at least $k$ filters. Experiments corroborate our theory: on a high-dimensional system, our predictor sharply outperforms prior methods at an equal parameter budget.

Systems and Control.title: Multi-objective Electric Vehicle Charging Strategies at Energy Hubs with Justice-informed Profit Distribution among Users
Systems and Control.summary: This paper studies potential energy cost savings in electric vehicle (EV) charging hubs when users allow cooperative vehicle-to-grid (V2G), and how such savings should be redistributed. To this end, we present multi-objective operational strategies and justice-informed profit sharing methods for a charging energy hub equipped with a battery storage system and solar panels. Specifically, we first frame the dynamic energy hub operational problem aiming to minimize a combination of grid costs and emissions, accounting for time-varying prices and energy mix as well as storage system and EV battery degradation, which is especially relevant when considering V2G operations. We parse the problem as a second-order conic program that can be efficiently solved to global optimality. Our real-world case-study shows the importance of flexibility for hub operation: Equipping a charging station with a stationary battery and leveraging dynamic V2G can significantly reduce the total costs and emissions compared to conventional settings without a battery or dynamic charging by more than 10%. To redistribute these cost benefits to users, we compare standard Nash bargaining with a justice-informed sufficientarian version which caps charging prices to safeguard adequate access to affordable charging. Our results show that the sufficientarian approach better accounts for inequalities in flexibility capital without significantly affecting aggregate costs, highlighting how justice-informed pricing only marginally affects total revenues.

Systems and Control.title: XIT: Exploration and Exploitation Informed Trees for Active Gas Distribution Mapping in Unknown Environments
Systems and Control.summary: Mobile robotic gas distribution mapping (GDM) provides critical situational awareness during emergency responses to hazardous gas releases. However, most systems still rely on teleoperation, limiting scalability and response speed. Autonomous active GDM is challenging in unknown and cluttered environments, because the robot must simultaneously explore traversable space, map the environment, and infer the gas distribution belief from sparse chemical measurements. We address this by formulating active GDM as a next-best-trajectory informative path planning (IPP) problem and develop XIT (Exploration and Exploitation Informed Trees), a sampling-based planner that grows a single shared tree toward multiple frontier goals, coupling exploration of unresolved regions with informative gas sampling en route. XIT draws a batch of samples from an Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) information field derived from the current gas posterior and expands the tree using a cost that trades off travel effort against information acquisition. To enable plume-aware exploration, we introduce the gas frontier concept, defined as unobserved regions adjacent to high gas concentrations, and propose the Wavefront Gas Frontier Detection (WGFD) algorithm for their identification. High-fidelity simulations demonstrate the benefits of XIT in terms of GDM quality and efficiency, and a scaled real-world experiment demonstrates its practicality. Although developed for active GDM, XIT is applicable to other robotic information-gathering tasks in unknown environments that face the exploration and exploitation trade-off.
Systems and Control.comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Robotics

Systems and Control.title: EMT Modeling and Coordinated Mode-Transition Ride-Through Control of Modern Data Centers
Systems and Control.summary: Large data centers are emerging as power-electronic loads whose response to grid voltage disturbances can affect bulk-system stability. This paper presents the composition and control characteristics of a proprietary electromagnetic transient (EMT) model of a modern data center comprising an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) with battery energy storage, induction-motor cooling loads, a computer room air handler (CRAH) driven by a variable-frequency drive (VFD), and an aggregated server load. A voltage-based state machine coordinates three aspects of the facility response: the UPS operating mode (eco, double conversion, or battery), the supply path of the CRAH, and a ramped reconnection of the grid-side UPS converter after the disturbance clears. A 100 MW facility is implemented in PSCAD/EMTDC and benchmarked against the PSSE PERC1 aggregate data center model under a symmetrical three-phase fault and low- and high-voltage ride-through (LVRT/HVRT) events. The two models agree closely in their voltage and active-power trajectories, while the EMT model also resolves the converter and motor-reacceleration transients that the phasor-domain model cannot.

Systems and Control.title: Spiking neuromodulation: a linear control perspective
Systems and Control.summary: Neuronal excitability is a nonlinear phenomenon, and the complexity of spiking experimental traces sometimes looks defeating. The present paper takes the view point that excitability is a neuromodulated property, and aims to demonstrate that the neuromodulation of spiking is amenable to the classical linear analysis tools of control theory. We illustrate the value of linear feedback analysis as an alternative to bifurcation analysis in the simple yet classical example of spiking modulation by the A-type potassium current.
Systems and Control.comment: 8 pages. Submitted to European Control Conference ECC 2027

Machine Learning.title: User Embeddings are Superpositions of Interpretable Behavioral Modes
Machine Learning.summary: User embeddings are central components of modern recommendation, personalization, and behavioral modeling systems. Though these embeddings can compactly encode rich behavioral information, they are inherently dense and opaque, limiting interpretability. To address this gap, we argue that user embeddings can be understood as sparse superpositions of interpretable behavioral modes. This structure is directly predicted by generative models of user behavior for linear embeddings and extends approximately to deep-learning representations by the superposition hypothesis. Superimposed modes can naturally be recovered by sparse dictionary learning methods, such as sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and recovered modes can be automatically named and queried in natural language. We validate mode recovery against known ground truth on synthetic data, where SAEs recover modes better than classical sparse baselines, including on transformer-encoded embeddings. We then apply the method to classical and transformer-based user embeddings from two real-world datasets. We also show how the corresponding natural-language labels enable zero-shot audience retrieval and characterization over embeddings never trained on text. The framework is post-hoc and model-agnostic, requiring no modification to the upstream embedding system.

Machine Learning.title: Selectivity and Shape in the Design of Forward-Forward Goodness Functions
Machine Learning.summary: The Forward-Forward (FF) algorithm trains networks layer-by-layer using a local "goodness function," yet the choice of activity statistic remains an important design question. We systematically study how selectivity and activity shape affect FF learning, introducing selective goodness functions based on top-$k$ and entmax-weighted energy alongside shape-sensitive objectives based on normalized higher-order moments. In particular, we propose burstiness goodness, a parameter-free, scale-invariant excess-kurtosis objective that rewards heavy-tailed activity patterns. Our study examines goodness functions together with activation and label-injection choices across six small-image datasets, and uses controlled experiments to isolate their effects. In validation-tuned, five-seed Fashion-MNIST experiments with matched ReLU activation, standard label injection, and per-layer scoring, burstiness improves accuracy from $73.2\pm0.9\%$ to $88.6\pm0.4\%$ over sum-of-squares. On CIFAR-10, burstiness improves block-local ResNet-18 accuracy from $28.9\pm0.5\%$ to $46.8\pm2.5\%$ under the same separate per-block label pathway. These results show that activity-shape statistics can provide effective local learning signals across the tested settings. Code is available at https://github.com/suayptalha/ff-selectivity-shape.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Main Track, poster). 16 pages, 1 figure

Machine Learning.title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists
Machine Learning.summary: AI-Scientists arrived, but a world for them to grow in did not. Human scientists take theirs for granted $-$ centuries of open problems and shared ideas, waiting in the scientific literature. To AI-Scientists, that world is readable but not runnable, so we build Scientist World for them: every research paper becomes an executable environment. Our autonomous pipeline extracts each paper's open-ended research question and reproduces its proposed method as the baseline; an AI-Scientist entering the environment is evaluated against what the human authors achieved. We release the first 1,000 verified environments. With the world as an evaluation, we found that frontier AI-Scientists can already surpass the human researchers 74% of the time. As a record of how AI does science, it contains 6,400 hours of research traces, with every idea, experiment, failure, and success. As a training ground, we are able to raise (+158%) a small model to match frontier models in research ideation. At last, AI-Scientists' own world has arrived, grown from and growing with science itself.

Machine Learning.title: XStack: A Benchmark for ML Repo Migration
Machine Learning.summary: ML code should run where researchers choose, not where it was first written. Today, machine learning code mainly lives in two ecosystems, PyTorch on NVIDIA GPUs and JAX on Google TPUs. Migrating repositories between them means building and testing across frameworks and hardware. This migration is (1) a practical need, since it unlocks different hardware for researchers, and (2) a natural benchmark: it involves different frameworks and hardware, covers whole repositories, and is long-horizon and challenging. We introduce XStack, a benchmark that evaluates agents on migrating ML repositories between these two ecosystems. Each agent receives a PyTorch repository and a clean TPU machine and must deliver a JAX repository. Its output passes if it meets our grading criteria, based on the source repository's published result, authenticated and calibrated by us. Migration by agents remains unreliable: Claude Opus 5 passes 75%, GPT-5.6-sol 45%, and every other agent at most 40%. XStack is a step toward freeing ML code from its ecosystem. We release XStack to make progress toward reliable migration across frameworks and hardware measurable.

Machine Learning.title: Same Behavior, Different Mechanism: What Finite Experiments Can Certify About Integrated Information
Machine Learning.summary: Interpretability, AI auditing and assessments of machine consciousness increasingly rest on mechanism-level quantities: functionals of a system's causal transition law that describe how it computes, not what it outputs. Experiments see that law only through finite, partial and noisy interventions. We ask when such a quantity is identifiable from an experiment's access, continuous in the mechanism and certifiable from finite data, and answer exactly for a deliberately demanding case - the integrated information $\varphi$ of integrated information theory - in stochastic networks of four and five units with known ground truth. Behavior can be silent: a recurrent and a feed-forward network with identical input-output laws at their response delay carry 0.28 and 0 bits, yet internal recordings separate them within 4-53 trials. Partial access can be just as blind: in our examples, units left out of a one-step recording impose precision floors of 0.30-1.02 bits that no sample size lowers, and in all-but-self parity networks, recordings of any length see several hidden units only through the product of their fidelities - a symmetry that one intervention broke in exact checks. The measure has sharp edges: because $\varphi$ selects a partition, and the cause and effect it specifies, by one criterion and reports another, infinitesimal changes of mechanism that cross an edge change it by 25-100% at 99% of the edges we found in random networks, and about 1% of surrogate models that fit interventional data almost perfectly misreport it by more than 20%. One-sided claims survive: the same data certify a lower bound on both sides of an edge, and we prove $\varphi>1.004$ bits throughout a 64-dimensional region of mechanisms and certify it from about $10^7$ controlled transitions with false-certificate probability at most $α$. Measurability is thus a design question with computable answers.
Machine Learning.comment: 30 pages, 7 figures. Code available as ancillary files

Machine Learning.title: Towards interpreting any residual stream direction by scaling activation inversion
Machine Learning.summary: To interpret a direction in a language model's residual stream, we can look for text that strongly activates it. But when such text is found by scanning a corpus, it is limited to what that corpus contains. We develop Maximally-Activating Example Metamodels (MAEMs), language models which map residual stream directions from a subject model to text exemplars that strongly activate those directions. Our objective is to maximise the cosine similarity of a supplied residual stream direction with the activations of the text generated by the MAEM. This label-free RL objective helps to scale MAEMs on diverse sources of residual stream directions. Empirically, we find the resultant metamodel produces informative exemplars: a Qwen3.6-27B MAEM inverts held-out activations better than corpus search or a natural-language autoencoder (NLA), beats corpus search (at 10M tokens) on a majority of held-out languages/domains, and activates 89% of held-out SAE features. It also identifies concepts behind steering vectors about as well as NLAs, recovers the payloads of LoRA backdoors more often than corpus search, and can even verbalise some model workspace inner monologue. Unlike explanations produced by other metamodels (e.g. NLAs), MAEM exemplars can be verified with a forward pass on the subject model, making the MAEM objective a grounded alternative for scaling the training of metamodels.
Machine Learning.comment: Euan Ong and Jiahai Feng advised equally

Machine Learning.title: Everything at Every Scale: Scale-Invariant Diffusion with Continuous Super-Resolution
Machine Learning.summary: Creating images from noise is image generation; reconstructing fine details from coarse inputs is super-resolution. Despite their practical differences, both can be understood as reversing information loss across scales. We introduce $\textbf{SKILD}$, a $\textbf{S}$cale-invariant $\textbf{K}$-Space $\textbf{I}$mage $\textbf{L}$earning $\textbf{D}$iffusion model that unifies generation and continuous super-resolution within a single unconditional framework. Both natural images and critical physical systems exhibit scale invariance, and we leverage it to design a forward process that attenuates image content from fine to coarse scales while injecting spectrum-matched Gaussian noise, making scale an explicit coordinate of the diffusion dynamics. The same trained reverse process performs generation and continuous super-resolution by varying only the starting timestep: $\textit{no task-specific architecture, no conditioning branch, no classifier-free guidance, no retraining per scale factor}$. Empirically, SKILD reaches FID $2.61$ and Inception Score $9.65$ on unconditional CIFAR-10, performs $2\times$--$8\times$ super-resolution on ImageNet from a single unconditional checkpoint while outperforming conditional models across perceptual metrics, and reconstructs critical Ising models whose connected four-point correlations closely track the ground truth.

Machine Learning.title: Adversarial Training with Large Step Sizes: Implicit Bias, Optimization, and Sharpness
Machine Learning.summary: Adversarial Training (AT) is an important method for improving model robustness. We study the dynamics of deterministic Gradient Descent (GD) in AT. Most existing works in this direction focus on the small or vanishing step sizes regime, where GD resembles a continuous-time flow. However, such step sizes can make training inefficient and are rarely used in practice. In this paper, we study the AT dynamics of GD with large constant step sizes. We first study GD in adversarial linear logistic regression, focusing on two aspects: where the model parameters converge (implicit bias) and how quickly the losses decrease (optimization). We then turn to neural networks training and study how the sharpness of losses evolve during AT. Our results advance the understanding of the behaviors of GD with large step sizes in AT and highlight three key differences from its behavior in Standard Training (ST): (i) the implicit bias gap between AT and ST, previously established only for small step sizes, persists for arbitrarily large constant step sizes, (ii) different from ST, there is no uniform rate of convergence for the optimization error in AT, and (iii) sharpness can exhibit two-stage dynamics that differ from the Edge-of-Stability behavior observed in ST.

Machine Learning.title: Unpacking the Compute Efficiency of Strong-to-Weak OPD against GRPO
Machine Learning.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher's per-token supervision. Does this dense signal reduce the training FLOPs needed to reach a target accuracy compared with reinforcement learning?
