Their electromagnetic coils pose a challenging design problem: they must reproduce the target magnetic field while satisfying engineering constraints and remaining practical and cost-effective to manufacture. Finding suitable geometries is a highly nonlinear inverse problem that generally has neither a closed-form nor a unique solution. This problem lies at the heart of stellarator design. We introduce CoilStellaration, a dataset and benchmark for learning the mapping between coil geometries from target plasma magnetic fields and engineering requirements. The dataset contains 177,000 optimized filamentary coilsets targeting plasma equilibria from ConStellaration, with sampled engineering requirements and achieved geometric and magnetic-field metrics. It spans multiple coil counts and field-period numbers, supporting studies of both specialized and shared models across configurations. The benchmark asks models to predict coils conditioned on a target equilibrium and requirements on coil-coil and coil-plasma spacing, curvature, and magnetic-field error. We show that magnetic-field accuracy remains the main challenge, with learned models rarely satisfying all requirements simultaneously. However, using learned predictions to initialize conventional coil optimization can accelerate early progress. We release baseline models and evaluation code to support reproducible research on both direct coil generation and learned optimization initializations. By lowering the barrier for machine learning and optimization researchers to engage with stellarator coil design, we aim to accelerate progress toward practical, cost-effective stellarator power plants.
Machine Learning.comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Track on Evaluations and Datasets

Machine Learning.title: Generative AI, Managerial Expectations, and Economic Activity
Machine Learning.summary: Using generative AI, we extract managers' economic expectations from over 120,000 corporate conference call transcripts. The resulting AI Economy Score predicts GDP growth, production, employment, and wages five or more quarters ahead, beyond survey forecasts and other existing measures. Industry- and firm-level scores capture sector- and firm-specific activity, and a composite of firm, industry, and macroeconomic expectations further improves forecasting power and horizon. Predictability concentrates among historically more accurate, less biased managers, consistent with an information rather than a noise channel. Managerial expectations thus offer incremental insights into economic activity, with implications for macro- and microeconomic decision-making.

Machine Learning.title: bispectrum: Selective G-Bispectra Made Practical
Machine Learning.summary: Many machine learning tasks are invariant under transformations such as translations and rotations. The $G$-bispectrum is a complete invariant that determines a signal up to a group action, but its computation is costly and existing implementations each cover a single group. We present bispectrum, an open-source, fully unit-tested PyTorch library providing efficient, differentiable selective $G$-bispectra for seven group actions. Selectivity reduces the number of coefficients from $O(|G|^2)$ to $O(|G|)$ for finite groups, from $O(m^{5/2})$ to $O(m)$ for planar rotations on the disk with $m$ harmonics, and from $Θ(L^3)$ to $Θ(L^2)$ for spherical 3D rotations using our augmented selective spherical bispectrum at band limit $L$. The library is invariant up to floating-point error and computes selective $G$-bispectra in sub-millisecond time on GPU. We evaluate them as pooling layers on PatchCamelyon and OrganMNIST3D against five baselines. Across 46 comparisons, bispectral pooling remains competitive, matching all baselines on PCam and improving on max pooling by 5.0 percentage points on OrganMNIST3D. On Spherical MNIST, our method with an MLP head reaches 95.8% on rotated test digits, matching a spherical CNN at $4\times$ lower latency and coming within 0.3 percentage points of a tensor-product network at $364\times$ lower latency. Selective $G$-bispectra provide fast, competitive invariant layers for finite and continuous groups.

Machine Learning.title: A four-step validation protocol for radiomic survival analysis in small cohorts: a body composition case study
Machine Learning.summary:
Gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (GEP-NET) lack prognostic biomarkers, and computed tomography (CT)-based body composition radiomics at the third lumbar vertebra (L3) is a promising candidate. Small cohorts make high-dimensional radiomic models prone to overfitting and single-split evaluations variable and optimistic.
  This methodological study proposes a four-step validation protocol for radiomic survival analysis in small cohorts: (1) false discovery rate (FDR)-corrected feature selection, (2) a dual-path comparison of prior feature selection versus embedded regularization, (3) repeated nested cross-validation (CV) and (4) a negative control with Gaussian noise features. In 78 GEP-NET patients, 535 radiomic features from five L3 compartments were used to evaluate five survival models with Harrell's concordance index (C-index), time-dependent area under the curve (AUC) and integrated Brier score (IBS).
  Step 1 selected at least one feature in 18% of outer folds under noise (nominal level 20%) versus 84% with radiomic features. The dual-path comparison showed no consistent difference between strategies. Repeated nested CV reduced variability across seeds (41% median reduction in C-index standard deviation), but not enough to distinguish models. The nested CV C-index exceeded chance by 0.07-0.15 with radiomic features but not clearly under noise (0.40-0.42 with prior feature selection, 0.47-0.55 with embedded regularization). Frequently selected features tentatively linked greater subcutaneous fat, skeletal muscle compactness and texture to better prognosis.
  These findings suggest a modest prognostic signal in L3 radiomics, with considerable uncertainty that the protocol quantifies. The protocol may transfer to other small-cohort radiomic survival studies. Code: https://github.com/marielatalaveram/radiomics-survival-validation-protocol.

Machine Learning.title: Library of Hands: Fix the Hands, Not the World Model
Machine Learning.summary: A world model predicts how a scene changes after an action, and a planner uses it to search for actions that reach a goal. If the camera moves or the controller changes, the same command moves the robot differently: when its commands are turned by 90 degrees, a frozen planner with the LeWM world model that succeeds in 77.5% of episodes succeeds in only 7.8%. Current fixes retrain the model, need training data, or forget a set-up when it returns. We propose Library of Hands (LoH), a training-free method that keeps the world model frozen and corrects only the map from commands to applied actions, which we call the hand. LoH reads the hand through the frozen model, with no extra sensor: it finds the action that best explains the change between two camera images (a reading). It stores every hand it identifies, so a returning set-up is recognised rather than re-learnt. In closed-loop tests, LoH more than doubles success on three simulated tasks, from 28.6% to 62.3%, and loses only 0.6 percentage points when nothing changes. It also works, unchanged, with two other world models and on two of three models pretrained on real robot data, and its gain grows with the quality of its readings.

Machine Learning.title: VLA Adaptation with Real and Simulated Data: A Case Study on Robotic Chess
Machine Learning.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are trained as general-purpose foundation models for robot learning, and require fine-tuning for each downstream task and robot. This raises practical questions such as how much data and training updates are needed, how checkpoints should be selected, and whether simulation can be leveraged to alleviate the cost of real data collection. We study these questions on a task that requires both precise manipulation and spatial understanding of the scene. In this task, an SO-101 arm moves a chess king between two squares that are given only by their names, such as e4 and a5. We fine-tune $π_{0.5}$ with various dataset sizes and update budgets, using teleoperated demonstrations as well as simulated demonstrations from a randomized scripted expert that imitates the variability of human demonstrations. In simulation, the success rate scales with both data and updates. Importantly, we find that a short learning-rate cool-down adds up to 31 points and is necessary for comparing checkpoints, and that validation loss and action error are unreliable for model selection. On the real arm, we fine-tune on up to 256 teleoperated demonstrations and evaluate ten policies in 25 trials each. Partial results indicate that pretraining on the simulated demonstrations helps substantially, most clearly when real data is scarce. We also present a negative result, in which training on the policy's own rollouts with filtered behavior cloning, RECAP-style advantage conditioning, corrections from an automatic coach, or residual reinforcement learning did not yield a measurable improvement over plain behavior cloning in our setting. We release the simulator, the expert and the real demonstrations.
Machine Learning.comment: CoRL 2026 Workshop "Pretrain to Adapt: What Makes a Pretrained Policy Adaptable?". 8 pages main text, 15 pages total, 15 figures, 4 tables

Machine Learning.title: Architecture-Dependent Causal Transfer of Activation States Across Large Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Direct communication between AI systems relies on natural language as an intermediate layer, incurring encoding/decoding overhead, token cost, and latency. We ask whether internal activation states can instead be transferred causally between different large language model (LLM) architectures via a learned projection, evaluated at three levels: representational similarity, cross-model retrieval from projected states, and end-to-end causal transfer via activation injection during generation. Using four architecturally diverse open-weight models (Qwen2-0.5B, Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B, FLAN-T5-base), we find that representational alignment in trained models exceeds a random-initialization null baseline and is best captured by a rank-based metric (mutual k-nearest-neighbour alignment), more robust to activation-magnitude outliers than centered kernel alignment (CKA) or Procrustes analysis. A learned projection network retrieves the correct target-model representation from a held-out set well above chance for the three causal decoder-only model pairs (45-50% top-1 accuracy vs. 5% chance) but at chance level for the encoder-based FLAN-T5. Injecting projected activations into a target model during generation produces a statistically significant, pre-registered causal effect on retrieval-based output similarity for only one of the three decoder-only pairs (Qwen2-0.5B to Phi-3-mini: 23.3% vs. 0.0% under negative control, p=0.047, FDR-corrected); the two pairs targeting Mistral-7B show no such effect despite comparable representational alignment at the hidden-state level. We interpret these results as evidence for causal transfer of the representational vehicle, not of meaning, and conclude that end-to-end activation-state transfer between LLMs, as currently implemented, is architecture-dependent rather than universal.
Machine Learning.comment: 13 pages, 3 tables. v2: code, data and logs released at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24088479; corrected three statements in the text of Section 4.1 (tables and conclusions unchanged)

Machine Learning.title: Controlled Binary Assignment Flows
Machine Learning.summary: This paper introduces a geometric approach to the representation and learning of time-variant parametrizations of deep assignment flows, for binary data labelings on graphs. Each edge carries an optimally controlled parameter flow in a 2-dimensional totally geodesic submanifold, based on objectives derived from a non-local linear scale space representation of the input data. The aggregation of triplets of such flows in 5-dimensional totally geodesic submanifolds is learned from data. The fusion of these flows determines the trajectory in the high-dimensional symmetric parameter space and by geometric integration the layers of binary deep assignment flows. Numerical results demonstrate the expressivity and the limitation of our highly parallel geometric local synthesis approach to high-dimensional deep assignment flow parametrizations.

Machine Learning.title: SCARCE: Scalable Cascade Analysis for Rare-event Characterisation via Embeddings
Machine Learning.summary: Rare events govern the safety profile of modern AI systems, yet their probabilities are extremely difficult to estimate: direct Monte Carlo requires prohibitive sample budgets. Subset Simulation (SS) addresses this by decomposing a rare-event probability into moderate conditional probabilities over nested intermediate events. However, classical SS requires a handcrafted scalar performance function whose sublevel sets define those events, demanding detailed knowledge of the failure geometry and limiting transfer to new domains. We propose SCARCE (Scalable Cascade Analysis for Rare-event Characterisation via Embeddings), which replaces the performance function with learned latent representations and geometric rulers that score proximity to failure regions. Adaptive thresholding constructs nested intermediate events directly from data. We formalise SCARCE through a non-negative supermartingale, yielding a high-probability upper envelope that remains valid under early stopping. On MNIST misclassification, where dense Monte Carlo provides ground truth, SCARCE achieves approximately 400--500 times lower mean absolute error than grid-searched traditional SS while eliminating systematic over-counting. We then study PAIR-style LLM jailbreaks under a fleet-level threat model with adversarial fraction $η$. On Llama-Guard-3-8B hidden states, a PCA-based ruler attains 2.6% mean relative error for $η\geq 10^{-3}$ against finite-sample references whose average bootstrap relative half-width is 27.9%, and transfers to a GCG-style corpus with 2.93% relative error after recalibration. A directional criterion $\mathrm{KL}(p_{\mathrm{good}}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{bad}})$ ranks rulers consistently with estimation error (Spearman $ρ=0.83$).

Machine Learning.title: Learn the Task, Not the Schedule: Reducing Spurious Cross-Arm Coupling in Bimanual Imitation Learning
Machine Learning.summary: A bimanual demonstration specifies both what the robot should do and one particular schedule for when each arm should act. Standard imitation learning does not distinguish task-required cross-arm constraints from incidental scheduling choices, and may therefore exploit opposite-arm progress as a shortcut cue, creating spurious cross-arm coupling even where relative timing is irrelevant for the current task phase. We introduce Constraint-preserving Temporal Recombination (CTR), a training-time data intervention that preserves recorded arm-local sensorimotor content while retiming the corresponding segments to realize admissible schedules that preserve task-required cross-arm constraints. We use CTR to train Diffusion Policy, Action Chunking with Transformers, and $π_{0.5}$, and evaluate them on four simulated and four real-robot tasks. Across six real-robot bimanual progress-state initializations, CTR raises worst-state success from 56% for the strongest non-CTR schedule mixture to 76%. With $π_{0.5}$ on an Independent task, a 4 s pause transfers 2.56 s of delay to the opposite arm under the Concurrent schedule distribution, but only 0.25 s with CTR. On real robots, CTR violates task constraints in only 0--4% of trials, versus 36--98% for narrow-schedule baselines. Code will be released at https://github.com/MINT-SJTU/CTR.

Machine Learning.title: Trade Promotion Optimisation for Consumer Goods
Machine Learning.summary: Trade promotions consume a large share of consumer-goods revenue, yet most planners still set discounts with a single, often unreliable, price elasticity per item. We present an end-to-end Trade Promotion Optimisation (TPO) system built as one chain: analogue SKUs, point elasticity, elasticity curve, price recommendation, promotional lift and net lift. Elasticity is measured at post-promo time from directional price-dip events against a rolling regular price, and at promo time by a causal estimator that residualises trend, seasonality and promotion, handles stock-out censoring with a Tobit likelihood and updates itself from the first clean promotion week. Items with weak evidence borrow the point elasticity and the curvature from analogue SKUs chosen by a cross-validated ridge model over category, brand, sub-category, price line and description. The optimiser separates self-price lift from substitution and post-promo dips and adjusts for inventory and trade funding. In a four-week promotion experiment on a 39-SKU consumer brand (mean elasticity -3.06), the plan lifts units by 20.6% and revenue by 6.9% at flat margin. Analogue pooling halves elasticity error relative to hierarchy averaging.

Machine Learning.title: A Mathematical Theory of Discursive Networks
Machine Learning.summary: Large language models (LLMs) turn writing into a live exchange between humans and software. We characterize this new medium as a discursive network that treats people and LLMs as equal nodes and tracks how their statements circulate. We define the generation of erroneous information as invalidation (any factual, logical, or structural breach) and show it follows four hazards: drift from truth, self-repair, fresh fabrication, and external detection. We develop a general mathematical model of discursive networks that shows that a network governed only by drift and self-repair stabilizes at a modest error rate. Giving each false claim even a small chance of peer review shifts the system to a truth-dominant state. We operationalize peer review with the open-source \emph{Flaws-of-Others (FOO) algorithm}: a configurable loop in which any set of agents critique one another while a harmonizer merges their verdicts. We identify an ethical transgression, epithesis, that occurs when humans fail to engage in the discursive network. The takeaway is practical and cultural: reliability in this new medium comes not from perfecting single models but from connecting imperfect ones into networks that enforce mutual accountability.

Machine Learning.title: Certify, Report, or Refuse: Harm-Constrained Conformal Prediction for Clinical Actions
Machine Learning.summary: Routing a melanoma case to routine follow-up is a serious action error that diagnostic coverage alone does not rule out. We present Harm-Constrained Risk-Optimal Conformal Prediction (HC-ROCP), a training-free framework that uses frozen classifier probabilities and adds a harm penalty when choosing prediction sets and actions. We test the resulting policies on disjoint calibration splits with multiplicity adjustment. HC-ROCP certifies supported claims, reports descriptive fallback policies, and refuses unsupported subgroup claims. We evaluate these outputs retrospectively on COVID-19 radiographs, ISIC 2019 dermoscopy, and EyePACS-to-APTOS retinopathy transfer. Across ten calibration seeds, HC-ROCP reduces COVID-19 severe-action errors from the exact risk-optimal baseline's 4.68\% to 0.54\%. At a 5\% budget, global claims are certified for COVID-19 and ISIC, but the rare squamous-cell-carcinoma claim is refused. At 1\%, all settings receive descriptive reports. For each budget, we also report the minimum severe-case count needed to pass the global harm gate with zero errors, providing a starting point for further data collection.
Machine Learning.comment: Findings of the 6th Machine Learning for Health Symposium (ML4H 2026)

Machine Learning.title: DPRM: A Plug-in Doob h transform-induced Token-Ordering Module for Discrete Diffusion Models
Machine Learning.summary: Discrete diffusion models admit many token orders, yet most systems rely on confidence-based decoding. Confidence is a strong and efficient heuristic, but it can be myopic because local certainty does not measure a position's effect on terminal quality. We introduce DPRM (Doob h-transform Process Reward Model), a plug-in token-ordering module induced by a terminal-reward-tilted trajectory distribution. The Doob transform converts terminal reward into a process reward for each candidate position. A compact estimator indexed by generation progress, confidence, and optional positional or task state makes this correction reusable across partial states. DPRM changes only token order; the host architecture, denoising objective, supervision, and token sampler remain fixed. We derive the exact reward-tilted law and bound its shortlist and online approximations. Across nine recent open-source hosts spanning language, multimodal generation, and scientific sequences, DPRM improves reasoning, numeric VQA, visual-codebook ordering, and preference-conditioned generation. Relative to confidence, it improves PUMA GSM8K by 14.6%, Omni-Diffusion CLIP-L/14 by 13.2%, Prism voted accuracy from 82.41% to 83.85%, and RealWorldQA numeric/count accuracy by 8.97 points. Matched scientific gains include 8.3% in DCM nonzero recovery, 15.0% in GenMol QED, and 53.3% in SDPO-DNA total utility. Entropy and random-order controls show that the gains do not come from favoring uncertain tokens indiscriminately. Token-order traces and shared-state interventions instead show how terminal reward can correct a locally confident but globally poor choice. Code is available at: https://github.com/DakeBU/DPRM-DLLM.

Machine Learning.title: Conformal Prediction for Distribution-to-Distribution Regression
Machine Learning.summary: Conformal Prediction (CP) provides a model-agnostic framework for constructing finite-sample prediction sets with coverage guarantees and has become a tool for reliable decision-making in high-risk settings. Recent advances have extended Split Conformal Prediction to increasingly complex learning problems, including multilabel, high-dimensional, and functional outputs. In this work, we study CP for Distribution-to-Distribution Regression, a setting of growing interest across many application domains. We show that a naive application of Split CP yields prediction sets that, while marginally valid, are non-interpretable, e.g., lacking a well-defined volume or a tractable sampling procedure, and of limited practical value. To overcome this, we propose a new conformal framework that operates in an orthogonal basis space, producing interpretable prediction sets while preserving coverage guarantees. We further develop an adaptive variant with asymptotic conditional coverage under mild assumptions. Empirical results on synthetic and real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/tuanhacs/conformal_d2d.

Machine Learning.title: Simulation-aided Reinforcement Learning with Control Variates
Machine Learning.summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms often rely on data collected from a target environment, which can be expensive and noisy. Although simulators can generate large amounts of additional data, standard simulation mixing approaches, which directly combine simulated and real experience, can degrade performance due to simulator inaccuracies, especially when they bias the solution away from the optimal policy. We propose a conservative simulation-aided learning method based on control variates, where simulated data is used solely to reduce variance in the learning process rather than directly shaping the learning target. We develop our approach for Policy-Evaluation, which is a fundamental building block of RL algorithms. Then we combine it within the actor-critic framework towards policy improvement, as well as extend it towards offline RL scenarios. Experiments on multiple MuJoCo benchmark tasks demonstrate improvements over standard simulation mixing approaches, highlighting control variates as an effective tool for simulation-aided reinforcement learning.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted as a poster at NeurIPS 2026. 10 pages main text + appendix, 3 figures. Code: https://github.com/OmerHemo/Simulation-Aided-Reinforcement-Learning-with-Control-Variates

Machine Learning.title: A Framework for Bounding Deterministic Risk with PAC-Bayes: Applications to Majority Votes
Machine Learning.summary: PAC-Bayes is a popular and efficient framework for obtaining generalization guarantees in situations involving uncountable hypothesis spaces. Unfortunately, in its classical formulation, it only provides guarantees on the expected risk of a randomly sampled hypothesis. This requires stochastic predictions at test time, making PAC-Bayes unusable in many practical situations where a single deterministic hypothesis must be deployed. We propose a unified framework for extracting guarantees for a single hypothesis from PAC-Bayesian guarantees. We present a general derandomization framework, and derive from it a numerical bound for majority votes and for three different probability distributions over the posterior space. We study the empirical behaviour of our approach, showing that it consistently outperforms popular baselines in terms of generalization bounds for single classifiers (by up to a factor of 2), but sometimes requires a sacrifice in accuracy.

Machine Learning.title: How Far Does Second-Order Linear Response Predict Quantization Mismatch? Pre-Registered Measurements on Five Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Serving systems choose a weight format for each model and deployment. A low-cost screen predicts the resulting KL divergence from the unquantized model's Fisher information using $\tfrac12Δ^\top FΔ$, the expansion underlying Hessian-aware and second-order post-training quantizers. We assess the reliability of this screen in GPU batches with channel-wise int8, per-tensor fp8 and group-wise int4 on Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-4B, OLMo-2-7B, Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-30B-A3B. Relative predictions hold across a 16-fold range of perturbation scales, int4 group sizes and rounding modes, while absolute predictions are heavy-tailed. A trimmed average brings 10 of 12 cells on Qwen3-4B and OLMo-2 within 15% of measured KL. The MoE model exhibits nonquadratic response at small perturbations, with int8 KL scaling as $α^{0.63}$. Computing per-sequence gradients in bf16 can cause fourfold prediction errors. We trace these errors to arithmetic in the lower half of the backward pass and eliminate them by using fp32 there. Batch-invariant kernels run at 0.55 times the throughput, while changes in reduction order introduce a floor of 0.17-0.22 nats per sequence. We build a screener with one streamed fp32 Fisher pass, trimmed tensor-block predictions with a band, a flag for aligned tensors and per-layer format allocation. On the unseen Mistral-7B-v0.3 family, all six predictions fall within the band, all three KL budgets are met, and vLLM throughput is predicted within 0.4%.

Machine Learning.title: Conditional Counterfactual Mean Embeddings: Doubly Robust Estimation and Learning Rates
Machine Learning.summary: A complete understanding of heterogeneous treatment effects requires fully capturing the conditional distribution of the counterfactual outcomes. To this end, we propose the Conditional Counterfactual Mean Embeddings (CCME), a framework that embeds conditional distributions of counterfactual outcomes into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). Under this framework, we develop a two-stage meta-estimator for CCME that accommodates any RKHS-valued regression in each stage. Based on this meta-estimator, we develop three practical CCME estimators: (1) Ridge Regression estimator, (2) Deep Feature estimator that parameterizes the feature map by a neural network, and (3) Neural-Kernel estimator that performs RKHS-valued regression, with the coefficients parameterized by a neural network. We provide finite-sample convergence rates for all estimators, establishing that they possess the double robustness property. Our experiments demonstrate that our estimators accurately recover distributional features including multimodal structure of conditional counterfactual distributions. Our code is available at https://github.com/donlap/Conditional-Counterfactual-Mean-Embeddings.

Machine Learning.title: HiFloat4 Format for End-To-End Reinforcement Learning Post-Training of Large Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: We present, to our knowledge, the first end-to-end FP4 RL post-training, in which both the rollout and training policies, including their forward and backward passes, operate at 4-bit precision. A systematic study reveals that the dominant source of degradation in FP4 RL is not training-side quantization error but rollout activation quantization: outliers stretch the dynamic range so far that a large number of activation values underflow to zero under FP4. Counterintuitively, restoring the training policy to higher precision while keeping the rollout in FP4 makes accuracy worse than full FP4 baseline, exposing rollout--training mismatch as the principal failure mode and ruling out standard pretraining-style fixes. We address this with Rollout Residual Quantization (Rollout-ResQ): a single residual correction term constrained to a hardware-friendly sparsity pattern, added only to the FP4 rollout matmul -- a lightweight correction that recovers most of the precision lost to outlier-driven underflow without inflating the rollout's compute footprint. On Qwen2.5-3B, Rollout-ResQ paired with the HiFloat4 (HiF4) format -- whose three-level hierarchical scaling preserves resolution under FP4's tight 4-bit budget -- closes the accuracy gap to BF16 from 3.59% to 1.39%, bringing fully quantized FP4 RL within close reach of full precision. Applied to the open-standard MXFP4, the same recipe narrows the gap from 13.6% to 5.3%, revealing that FP4 format choice is a key factor that determines the ceiling on recoverable accuracy. The experimental results on Qwen2.5-Math-7B further confirm the recovery benefits of Rollout-ResQ with HiF4. Together, these results establish HiF4 as the enabling format for end-to-end FP4 RL post-training, and Rollout-ResQ as the activation-side mechanism that makes the gap to BF16 closable.

Machine Learning.title: Spike-to-Field Mechanisms of Turbulence-Like Dynamics in Spatial Spiking Neural Networks
Machine Learning.summary: Neural avalanches and turbulence-like brain dynamics are usually measured after neural activity has been coarse-grained into continuous fields, leaving open which spike-level mechanisms can generate these macroscopic observables. We build a spatial leaky integrate-and-fire spiking neural network and explicitly transform spikes into activity-density and Hilbert phase fields. A delayed, distance-dependent, passive-dendrite regime reproducibly generates turbulence-like field structure, including high-amplitude phase-defect tracks, structure-function scaling, and power-law-favored continuous-field avalanche tails. Controls show that firing rate, vortex count, and avalanche tail fits are individually insufficient: destroying delayed propagation, dendritic filtering, or spike timing suppresses key field signatures, while random-space nulls can retain many mathematical phase defects but show weaker spatial structure and synaptic-delay transfer. Biologically motivated gates further shape the regime: PV-like perisomatic inhibition clamps phase dynamics, SST-like dendritic inhibition and projection-specific inhibitory facilitation preserve long-lived tracks, and a rate-constrained projection-STP regime expresses a roughly 200-ms episode at 12.25 Hz (full-record mean) across 12 seeds. These results use SNNs as a mechanistic testbed for spike-derived brain turbulence observables and show why phase defects and avalanche-like statistics must be interpreted jointly with spatial scaling and spike-level propagation.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 23 pages, including references, appendices, and checklist

Machine Learning.title: Memorization and Malign Generalization in Conditional Diffusion Models with Random Features
Machine Learning.summary: Conditional diffusion models generate diverse, novel, and high-quality samples under prescribed conditions. However, theoretical understanding of their memorization and generalization remains limited, while recent works have characterized these behaviors primarily in unconditional settings. In this work, we analyze a random-feature conditional score model in the high-dimensional proportional limit, deriving asymptotic expressions for training and test losses. By decomposing the test loss, we show that in the overparameterized regime, increasing model width improves prediction of the condition-dependent mean while reducing within-condition prediction variance, a phenomenon we term "malign generalization." We further show that in the infinite-width limit, the model predicts the conditional mean as accurately as ridge regression of the data on the condition, while its within-condition variance vanishes. Finally, analyzing the training loss reveals that more informative conditions lead to memorization of training samples at smaller widths. These theoretical findings are supported by experiments with U-Net architectures on realistic data.

Machine Learning.title: When Does LeJEPA Learn a World Model?
Machine Learning.summary: A representation that scrambles the true degrees of freedom of the world cannot support reliable planning or compositional generalization. We prove that LeJEPA (alignment plus Gaussian regularization) linearly recovers the world's latent variables from nonlinear observations, a property known as linear identifiability, in a class of worlds where latents evolve under stationary, additive-noise transitions. Our main result is that among all such worlds, the Gaussian is the unique latent distribution for which this guarantee holds. The forward direction rests on a spectral decomposition in which each degree of nonlinearity is strictly penalized by alignment, making the linear map the optimum; the converse rules out every non-Gaussian alternative. We further prove an approximate identifiability result where the guarantee degrades gracefully, and show that linear, orthogonal identifiability enables optimal latent-space planning. We validate the theory with experiments ranging from 2D examples to 4096-dimensional latents, including ablations, pixel-based robotic control, and natural images from ImageNet-X. Our theory turns an empirically successful recipe into a mathematical guarantee, providing the foundation for building World Models that provably recover the structure of the world.
Machine Learning.comment: NeurIPS 2026 camera-ready. 52 pages, 22 figures, 14 tables. Code: https://github.com/klindtlab/lejepa-identifiability

Machine Learning.title: FFM-CP: Cross-Backbone Fusion of Vision-Language Foundation Models for Few-Shot Computational Pathology
Machine Learning.summary: Pathology vision-language foundation models vary in performance across diseases and tasks, with no single model consistently performing best. The high cost of expert pathology annotation can also limit the labeled data available for task-specific adaptation. Combining complementary pretrained representations is a potential approach to these limitations, yet learning an effective fusion from few labeled examples remains challenging. We introduce Few-shot Fusion Foundation Models of Computational Pathology (FFM-CP), which is a framework that combines multiple pathology vision-language models in the few-shot learning setting. The framework first aligns heterogeneous representations using a closed-form Orthogonal Procrustes transformation estimated from corresponding support images. This alignment preserves within-model feature geometry without training an additional alignment network. Within the aligned space, a unified graph enables information exchange across backbones by jointly refining support-image features and visual and textual class prototypes. These refined representations support complementary text-prototype and case-retrieval branches that capture semantic class knowledge and within-class visual variation, respectively. Each branch learns to combine predictions from all ordered backbone pairs, allowing queries encoded by one model to draw on evidence represented by another. We evaluate three backbone combinations on six histopathology datasets at 4, 8, and 16 shots per class. FFM-CP achieves higher mean macro-F1 than the strongest individually adapted member of each fused set in 50 of 54 comparisons. These findings suggest that combining complementary pretrained representations can improve histopathological classification when annotations are limited.

Machine Learning.title: Double Blind Evals: Resolving the Dual Confidentiality Dilemma in AI Safety Auditing
Machine Learning.summary: AI safety evaluations often involve sensitive prompts and proprietary models. Evaluators want to keep their evaluation prompts secret from model owners to prevent purposeful or incidental data leakage, ensuring longer usefulness of their benchmark. Model owners in turn wish to keep their proprietary model weights and inference code within their own secure infrastructure to protect their IP. We present a way forward for "double-blind evals", which provide cryptographic guarantees that an evaluator's prompts are not shared with the model owner, while simultaneously maintaining the confidentiality of the model weights and inference code. To accomplish this, we use secure enclaves that encrypt data in RAM at the hardware level. In a world-first pilot, we test this approach by evaluating a proprietary Google DeepMind model (Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite) against a selection of the private AILuminate benchmark corpus, using an NVIDIA H100 secure enclave on Google Cloud Platform, and using OpenMined's PySyft to maintain data and model privacy. We believe this effort marks the first use of this technology to provide mutual secrecy for one organization's frontier-class proprietary model weights and another organization's closed benchmark.

Machine Learning.title: OCELOT: Planetary-Scale Species Distribution Modeling with Satellite Foundation Embeddings
Machine Learning.summary: Large-scale repositories of species observations now contain billions of occurrence records from around the world, but these sightings cluster heavily in human-accessible areas. Existing models use only a small fraction of these records and are not evaluated on extrapolating to remote, unvisited regions--where species distribution models can be used as geographic priors to help classify data from camera traps and acoustic recorders. We scale relative occurrence species distribution models by training a multimodal implicit neural representation network called OCELOT that fuses spatial coordinates with satellite foundation embeddings on two orders of magnitude more observations than previous work: 2 billion GBIF records across 100,000 taxa. Scaling to this regime requires co-designing the data pipeline, taxonomic representation, loss formulation, and model architecture: spatiotemporal thinning and sub-linear cell sampling correct for spatial redundancy and observer bias, while an additive taxonomic readout shares representations across species, genera, and families to improve predictions for rare taxa. To evaluate performance in remote areas, we benchmark geographic extrapolation using the NDCG metric on spatial block holdouts up to 600 km. Satellite foundation embeddings improve extrapolation by 51% over coordinate-only models and outperform classical bioclimatic rasters. The resulting model also matches or outperforms existing baselines on established interpolation benchmarks, demonstrating that optimizing for geographic extrapolation does not compromise in-distribution accuracy.

Machine Learning.title: TRACE: Adaptive Trust-Region Bayesian Optimization for Open-Ended Molecular Design
Machine Learning.summary: Optimizing molecules under small evaluation budgets requires deciding both where in chemical space to search and which candidate within that region to evaluate. We introduce Trust Region Adaptive Chemical Exploration (TRACE), a framework for open-ended molecular Bayesian optimization (BO), where candidates are generated on demand rather than selected from a fixed library. TRACE combines an objective-free graph-perturbation mechanism with a fixed, chemistry-aware Gaussian process (GP) surrogate using fragprints, a representation combining molecular fingerprints and fragment descriptors. Rather than learning the search geometry itself, TRACE makes the scale of chemical exploration explicit through a Tanimoto-similarity threshold controlling chemical extent and a cardinality budget controlling candidate-search breadth. A simple success/failure controller expands or contracts both quantities during optimization, while the GP and acquisition function select which admissible molecules to evaluate. Across six challenging molecular optimization benchmarks under matched 1,000-evaluation budgets, TRACE achieves the strongest overall sample efficiency as measured by the best molecule found as evaluations accumulate. Crossed ablations on two objectives further show that adaptive region control contributes beyond the proposal mechanism, while its benefit depends on the proposal distribution. We further apply TRACE to the stability of iron phthalocyanine (FePc), a non-precious molecular electrocatalyst whose degradation can involve loss of the Fe center. Using a first-principles density functional theory (DFT) workflow designed for accurate energy evaluation, TRACE increases the computed thermodynamic resistance to Fe dissolution from 0.42 to 2.59 eV over 80 designed evaluations.

Machine Learning.title: From Likelihood Convergence to Parameter Convergence in POMDPs
Machine Learning.summary: Likelihood-based methods are widely used to learn the parameters of partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). While finite-sample guarantees for policy suboptimality exist for certain POMDP subclasses, analogous guarantees for parameter recovery remain less well understood. For any candidate POMDP parameter, we bound its parameter recovery error in terms of its likelihood gap to the ground truth, the structural conditioning of the observation and transition kernels, and the behavior policy used to collect data. The bound applies in both the undercomplete and overcomplete regimes, with the latter following naturally from the undercomplete analysis. Because the result applies to any sufficiently good candidate, it yields finite-sample guarantees for the maximum-likelihood estimator and any procedure producing a parameter with controlled likelihood gap. This is particularly useful for near-optimal learning in infinite-horizon POMDPs, where existing approaches largely rely on model-based planning with accurate transition and observation kernel estimates. The bound separates the contributions of the behavior policy and model, showing how data-collection choices, including action coverage, and their effects on mixing can accelerate parameter learning.

Machine Learning.title: Evaluating Cross-Signal Coherence in Mammography Vision-Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: As vision-language models (VLMs) move toward interpreting medical images directly, their outputs increasingly include not just a label but a stated confidence and a written justification. Yet the field still predominantly evaluates VLMs using just accuracy. We evaluate the coherence between answer, confidence, and explanation across four VLMs on breast density and BI-RADS categorization, using two mammography datasets. We perform controlled perturbations of the question, multiple choice option orders, and the images and assess changes in the three outputs. Our results suggest confidence does not decrease even as the mammography image is changed. Shuffling the options also changes most VLMs' answers. Notably, there are cases where a model's own stated reasoning contradicts its final answer, a distinction accuracy alone cannot capture but one that governs whether an AI-generated answer can be trusted.

Machine Learning.title: NPCNet: Navigator-Driven Pseudo Text for Deep Clustering of Early Sepsis Phenotyping
Machine Learning.summary: Sepsis is a heterogeneous syndrome. Identifying clinically distinct phenotypes may enable more precise treatment strategies. In recent years, many researchers have applied clustering algorithms to sepsis patients. However, many existing approaches require aggregating or imputing temporal Electronic Health Records (EHRs), which can limit the model's ability to capture disease progression. Furthermore, existing clustering processes seldom incorporate domain-driven constraints, often resulting in phenotypes that lack clear clinical distinction. We propose a novel clustering network, NPCNet, that comprises a text embedding generator, a clustering operator, and a target navigator. We first transformed EHRs into pseudo texts by discretizing continuous clinical measurements and integrated them with static variables to construct the embeddings. The target navigator then infused clinical knowledge into the embeddings through auxiliary tasks, constraining clustering results to better align sepsis phenotypes with clinical significance. Finally, the clustering operator employed an iterative refinement mechanism to jointly optimize phenotype centroids and patient representations under domain-driven constraints. Extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrated that NPCNet achieved superior performance on both internal clustering and clinical metrics. We identify four distinct sepsis phenotypes with divergent SOFA trajectories. Notably, although α and δ exhibit similarly severe conditions initially, NPCNet distinguishes patients likely to improve (α) from those at risk of deterioration (δ). Furthermore, treatment effect analysis suggests that early vasopressor administration may be associated with improved outcomes in the α, \{beta}, and δ phenotypes. These findings highlight NPCNet's potential for phenotype-specific treatment strategies.

Machine Learning.title: LawKAN: Group-Law Layers for Composition -- When Imposing a Known Law Pays Off
Machine Learning.summary: Many tasks compose transformations by a known rule: chained rotations in robotics and navigation. Learned models relearn it, compounding error; classical estimators hardcode it and miss hardware deviations. We impose the known structure and learn only the remainder: an exact non-commutative group law sits in the node of a self-contained layer, its edges learn local increments, and a zero-initialized correction psi learns unknown deviations of the law. A pre-training criterion predicts exact representability. On fixed-angle SU(2) composition, a 54-parameter dense edge is the most accurate dense model, at 27x fewer parameters than the strongest fixed-matrix baseline, and lies 0.05 deg above the Bayes floor. On real robot arms, an isolated 306-parameter psi reaches 1.12-1.14 mm versus 1.29-1.33 mm for Gauss-Newton at N >= 60, and the recipe transfers across three vendors and two protocols. The recipe matches classical fits where the data obey the law and loses where the imposed law is not the task's.
Machine Learning.comment: 20 pages main text (53 total), 15 figures, 6 tables in main text (31 incl. appendices). Code: https://github.com/occamolab/lawkan

Machine Learning.title: Correctness vs Efficiency: Behavior Control with Weight-Space Extrapolation in Code RL
Machine Learning.summary: A model trained with an imperfect reward in RL may learn to exploit the reward with undesired behavior. We study a controlled form of this problem in competitive programming. A program may pass small tests while violating the intended efficiency requirement on larger inputs. We construct a family of rewards that progressively relax the efficiency constraint, making the reward increasingly easy to exploit, and train separate policies. This sweep reveals a correctness-efficiency frontier. Relaxing the reward leads to less efficient programs and more resource-limit failures. Stricter rewards suppress these failures but increase correctness failures near the model's capability boundary. This frontier is also reflected in weight space. Interpolating between the resulting models reproduces the same behavioral change. More surprisingly, extrapolation in both directions further amplifies or suppresses it beyond the trained checkpoints. Extensive experiments show that this pattern holds across pure reasoning, tool use, and agentic coding, and at both 32B and 7B scales. This suggests a simple intervention for this form of reward hacking: use a loose reward to amplify the undesired behavior, use the weight-space difference to a strict-reward model as its steering vector, and then extrapolate past the strict model to suppress it.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Camera-ready version, 54 pages

Machine Learning.title: Hierarchical Conformal Classification
Machine Learning.summary: Conformal prediction (CP) is a powerful framework for quantifying uncertainty in machine learning models, offering reliable predictions with finite-sample coverage guarantees. When applied to classification, CP produces a prediction set of possible labels that is guaranteed to contain the true label with high probability, regardless of the underlying classifier. However, standard CP treats classes as flat and unstructured, ignoring domain knowledge such as semantic relationships or hierarchical structure among class labels. This paper presents hierarchical conformal classification (HCC), an extension of CP that incorporates class hierarchies into both the structure and semantics of prediction sets. We formulate HCC as a constrained optimization problem whose solutions yield prediction sets composed of nodes at different levels of the hierarchy, while maintaining coverage guarantees. To address the combinatorial nature of the problem, we formally show that a much smaller, well-structured subset of candidate solutions suffices to ensure coverage while upholding optimality. An empirical evaluation on three new benchmarks consisting of audio, image, and text data highlights the advantages of our approach, and a user study shows that annotators significantly prefer hierarchical over flat prediction sets.

Machine Learning.title: Challenges in Non-Polymeric Crystal Structure Prediction: Why a Geometric, Permutation-Invariant Loss is Needed
Machine Learning.summary: Crystalline structure prediction is an essential prerequisite for designing materials with targeted properties. Yet, it is still an open challenge in materials design and drug discovery. Despite recent advances in computational materials science, accurately predicting three-dimensional non-polymeric crystal structures remains elusive. In this work, we focus on the molecular assembly problem, where a set~$\mathcal{S}$ of identical rigid molecules is packed to form a crystalline structure. Such a simplified formulation provides a useful approximation to the actual problem. However, while recent state-of-the-art methods have increasingly adopted sophisticated techniques, the underlying learning objective remains ill-posed. We propose a better formulation that introduces a loss function capturing key geometric molecular properties while ensuring permutation invariance over $\mathcal{S}$. Remarkably, we demonstrate that within this framework, a simple regression model already outperforms prior approaches, including flow matching techniques, on the COD-Cluster17 benchmark, a curated non-polymeric subset of the Crystallography Open Database (COD). Our code is available at https://github.com/inria-thoth/SinkFast.

Machine Learning.title: Conformal PM2.5 Mapping Under Spatial Covariate Shift: Satellite-Reanalysis Fusion for Africa's Green Industrial Transition
Machine Learning.summary: Africa's green industrialization imperative demands reliable infrastructure for monitoring air quality. We present a satellite-reanalysis PM2.5 fusion system trained on 2,068,901 records from 404 monitoring locations in 29 African countries (OpenAQ, 2017-2022), combining LightGBM with leakage-resistant spatial cross-validation and conformal prediction to quantify predictions and their geographic applicability limits. Under 5-fold location-grouped spatial cross-validation, LightGBM achieves RMSE = 30.83 +/- 5.07 ug/m3, MAE = 14.54 +/- 1.66 ug/m3, R2 = 0.134 +/- 0.023, and macro F1 = 0.336 +/- 0.018. This R2 is substantially below random-split benchmarks (>0.90) but reflects true geographic generalisation difficulty rather than model failure. Split conformal prediction targeting 90% marginal coverage reveals severe East Africa degradation (actual PICP = 65.3% vs. nominal 90%), consistent with medium-strength covariate shift (humidity KS = 0.2237, sat_pblh KS = 0.2558). We operationalise these findings through regional reliability flags (High/Medium/Low/Unreliable) and a monitor prioritisation score directing infrastructure expansion toward highest-burden unmonitored populations, directly supporting Africa's green industrial transition and SDGs 3.9, 7.1.2, 9, 11.6.2, and 13.
Machine Learning.comment: 9 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables. Index Terms: PM2.5 mapping, conformal prediction, covariate shift, spatial cross-validation, air quality, green industrialisation, trustworthy AI, Africa

Machine Learning.title: A Strict Upper Bound for Three-Point Weighted Selection in Planar Vector-Valued Regression
Machine Learning.summary: We prove $F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,3)<11/6$ for minimum-Frobenius-norm least-squares regression with two input and two output coordinates, improving the upper bound $15/8$. More precisely, a universal $\varepsilon_0>0$ satisfies $\mathcal T_3\le(5/6-\varepsilon_0)E$ for every finite residual frame. The proof combines an exact scalar certificate, rigidity of equality in planar selection, and a compactness argument that controls disappearing weights. Together with the known lower bound, this gives $13/8\le F_{\mathrm{weighted}}(2,2,3)<11/6$. No numerical value of $\varepsilon_0$ is claimed.

Machine Learning.title: Learning inexact alternating minimization for convex problems with quadratic coupling
Machine Learning.summary: Alternating minimization is a standard tool for optimization problems with two coupled variable blocks. Its cost is dominated by the inner subproblem solvers, which rarely have a closed-form solution. In this paper, we propose to learn an inexact alternating scheme in which neural networks approximate the subproblem solution at each iteration. For convex problems with quadratic couplings between the variable blocks that satisfy a quadratic growth condition, we derive a worst-case bound on the optimality gap that exposes the per-iteration error that each network is trained to minimize in a greedy fashion. Combining the bound with a PAC-Bayes argument, we obtain a fixed-horizon, high-probability bound on the expected optimality gap over the distribution of problem instances. We apply the learned scheme to robust matrix completion and low-dose CT reconstruction with dictionary regularization where we achieve a 5x-13x speedup over the inexact first-order baseline at matched accuracy. A brief end-to-end fine-tuning stage extends this up to 30x and outperforms other learned schemes. The code is available at https://github.com/paulhausner/learned-alternating-minimization.

Machine Learning.title: Improving Evaluation Realism with Inference-Time Compute and Deployment Scaffolds
Machine Learning.summary: A core obstacle to alignment evaluation is evaluation awareness: capable models can tell when they are being tested rather than deployed, weakening the conclusions a safety evaluation can support. We present two techniques that make simulated alignment evaluations harder to distinguish from real deployments. Our first technique, critique refinement, spends additional inference-time compute on each simulator action: the simulator generates multiple candidate actions, refines them using feedback from an instance of the target model on how to make them more realistic, and continues the evaluation with the most deployment-like candidate. Our second technique, DISH (Deployment-Imitating SWE-Agent Harness), wraps the target in an agent harness, reducing the gap between simulated and real deployment environments in coding settings. We test the techniques on multiple target models and find that applying both yields larger realism gains than either alone. We show that automated approaches can improve the realism of alignment evaluations, and that they compare favorably to spending the extra compute on more audit attempts.
Machine Learning.comment: 78 pages, 45 figures, 6 tables (8 figures in the main text). Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Code: https://github.com/meridianlabs-ai/petri_dish and https://github.com/AxelAhlqvist1995/petri-bon ; reproduction assets: https://github.com/AxelAhlqvist1995/petri-realism-reproduction

Machine Learning.title: Diffusion LLMs are Natural Adversaries for any LLM
Machine Learning.summary: We introduce a novel framework that transforms the resource-intensive (adversarial) prompt optimization problem into an \emph{efficient, amortized inference task}. Our core insight is that pretrained, non-autoregressive generative LLMs, such as Diffusion LLMs, which model the joint distribution over prompt-response pairs, can serve as powerful surrogates for prompt search. This approach enables direct conditional generation of prompts, effectively replacing costly discrete optimization with a small number of parallelizable samples. We provide a probabilistic analysis demonstrating that under mild fidelity assumptions, only a few conditional samples are required to recover high-reward (harmful) prompts. Empirically, our method substantially outperforms prior attacks in both success rate and compute cost, producing low-perplexity, diverse jailbreaks that transfer to a wide range of black-box target models, including robustly trained and proprietary LLMs. Beyond adversarial prompting, our framework opens new directions for red teaming, automated prompt optimization, and leveraging emerging Flow- and Diffusion-based LLMs.

Machine Learning.title: K-prop: Deep Online Learning by Backpropagating Temporal Kernels
Machine Learning.summary: Self-recurrence represents an important component for temporal processing in neural networks, both artificial and biological, where it appears naturally in the form of leaky integration. However, due to the complex temporal dependencies of the gradient, an efficient and effective method of online training is still lacking. Here we propose K-prop, a novel online learning method for leaky neural networks. It dramatically reduces the computational and memory cost of real time recurrent learning (RTRL) by propagating kernel gains. K-prop also outperforms existing RTRL approximations and achieves performance comparable to backpropagation through time in sequence learning, classification, and reinforcement learning tasks. We further analyze how its sole approximation affects gradient quality and identify conditions under which K-prop remains accurate and effective.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted for publication in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 40 (NeurIPS 2026)

Machine Learning.title: Can the Confidence and Decisions of System 1 Models Be Trusted? An Explainability and Perturbation Audit of Jev-Style Decision Models
Machine Learning.summary: "System 1" decision models (pioneered by TypeSafe AI's Jev) replace autoregressive text generation with a single forward pass returning typed probability distributions over declared schemas (Choice, Score, Noul). While deployed for low-latency routing and automated triage, their statistical calibration and post-hoc explainability remain uncharacterized. We introduce an open, deterministic audit benchmark evaluating System 1 decision models across calibration under label-preserving perturbations, cross-question interference, and post-hoc attribution faithfulness. Evaluating five open-weight models (0.8B to 27B) alongside generative System 2 baselines -- both single-token logprob scoring and structured JSON/CoT decoding -- across NLI (e-SNLI), adversarial syntactic shortcuts (HANS), synthetic clinical triage (N=900), prompt injection defense (Tensor Trust, N=250), and an 86-case logic-gate trigger suite yields five findings: (1) provider confidence is an exact closed-form dispersion transform (1 - H(p)/ln K on sub-10B models; normalized margin on Clef-27B) rather than empirical accuracy; (2) bundling multiple questions in one request induces directional cross-question interference (11.7% to 22.4% binary flips on Tev1-0.8B, vs. 0.1% to 0.2% on Tev1-4B); (3) System 1 models with >= 4B parameters are faster and better calibrated under syntactic shifts (ECE_w = 0.030 to 0.087) than logprob (0.144) and JSON (0.378) baselines; (4) for prompt-injection defense (N=250), >= 4B models achieve 0.988 to 0.998 AUROC with up to 95.2% recall and 0.0% false alarms at 48 to 60 ms; and (5) single-pass inference makes 512-coalition XAI interactive (1.3 to 3.2 s/input), while KernelSHAP with a logit link (S1-SHAP) mitigates softmax saturation on disjunctive OR gates (89.3% to 100.0% gate recovery vs. 57.1% to 82.1% in prob space; p_adj = 0.004).
Machine Learning.comment: 36 pages, 4 figures, 16 tables. Code and benchmark artifacts available at https://github.com/j2launay/jev-decision-models-xai

Machine Learning.title: Towards Multi-Source Domain Generalization for Sleep Staging with Noisy Labels
Machine Learning.summary: Automatic sleep staging is a multimodal learning problem involving heterogeneous physiological signals such as EEG and EOG, which often suffer from domain shifts across institutions, devices, and populations. In practice, these data are also affected by noisy annotations, yet label-noise-robust multi-source domain generalization remains underexplored. We present the first benchmark for Noisy Labels in Multi-Source Domain-Generalized Sleep Staging (NL-DGSS) and show that existing noisy-label learning methods degrade substantially when domain shifts and label noise coexist. To address this challenge, we propose FF-TRUST, a domain-invariant multimodal sleep staging framework with Joint Time-Frequency Early Learning Regularization (JTF-ELR). By jointly exploiting temporal and spectral consistency together with confidence-diversity regularization, FF-TRUST improves robustness under noisy supervision. Experiments on five public datasets demonstrate consistent state-of-the-art performance under diverse symmetric and asymmetric noise settings.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted to the MLESP 2026 workshop (The 7th international workshop on Machine Learning for EEG Signal Processing) in conjunction with IEEE BIBM 2026

Machine Learning.title: UniHam: A Large-Scale SOC-Complete Dataset and Benchmark for Hamiltonian Learning in Materials
Machine Learning.summary: Accurate prediction of electronic Hamiltonians would enable broad property inference while avoiding the high computational cost of Density Functional Theory (DFT). However, progress toward general-purpose materials foundation models is limited by a data bottleneck: existing Hamiltonian datasets are typically small, lack structural diversity, and often omit essential relativistic physics such as spin--orbit coupling (SOC). We therefore construct UniHam, a large-scale Hamiltonian dataset and benchmark suite comprising 100,000+ DFT-computed complex-valued Hermitian Hamiltonians with full SOC, covering 72 elements and a wide range of crystal geometries and symmetries (spanning diverse lattice types and space-group families). Building on UniHam, we benchmark two representative state-of-the-art models under a standardized protocol and introduce complementary evaluation metrics that jointly assess three dimensions: (i) Hamiltonian reconstruction accuracy, (ii) out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization across composition/symmetry shifts, and (iii) the ability to support downstream property prediction from the predicted Hamiltonians. Experiments on UniHam demonstrate that the proposed benchmark and metrics effectively differentiate model capabilities, revealing intrinsic SOC- and element-dependent failure modes, large variations in compositional OOD robustness, and the necessity of spectral-level evaluation to assess whether Hamiltonian predictions reliably support downstream electronic-structure properties. Overall, UniHam provides a reproducible, SOC-complete benchmark that can sharpen model comparisons and accelerate the development of next-generation foundation models for quantum materials.

Machine Learning.title: ManifoldCache: Training-Free Diffusion Acceleration via Constraint Manifold Caching
Machine Learning.summary: Diffusion models for structured scientific generation must produce samples satisfying hard geometric constraints imposed by physics, chemistry, or biology, yet inference in these settings is prohibitively slow, demanding hundreds to thousands of neural-function evaluations per sample. We unify eight state-of-the-art models spanning medical volumetrics, molecular conformations, protein backbone design, crystal structure prediction, and multi-view 3D scenes under a single abstraction, Constraint-Manifold Diffusion Models (CMDMs), in which the target distribution is supported on a manifold defined by an externally specified constraint map. All existing acceleration families fail on this class: quantization exhausts memory on high-dimensional volumetric operators; pruning breaks constraint fidelity; fast ODE solvers allow trajectories to drift off the constraint manifold; and feature-caching heuristics are blind to constraint geometry, inducing mode confusion in the high-noise regime. We introduce ManifoldCache, the first training-free, data-free accelerator designed from first principles for CMDMs. The key insight is that the conditional score decomposes orthogonally into a normal component, which enforces constraint satisfaction, and a tangential component, which navigates within the manifold. Exploiting this structure, we prove that the noise-schedule midpoint is a sharp safe-caching boundary: caching before it incurs provably bounded error, while caching after it guarantees a strictly positive fraction of trajectories suffer mode confusion, a gap that persists up to the boundary. We further prove that deeper network blocks admit provably larger certified cache strides within the safe phase, as a consequence of the score decomposition propagating through block Jacobians. The resulting schedule requires no calibration data, along with zero training overhead.

Machine Learning.title: ANCORA: Learning to Question via Manifold-Anchored Self-Play for Verifiable Reasoning
Machine Learning.summary: We propose a paradigm shift toward open-ended curriculum self-play: rather than learning to answer on a fixed prompt set, a unified policy learns to question: generating verifiable problems, solving them, and turning verifier feedback into self-improvement. We introduce ANCORA, in which the policy alternates between a Proposer that synthesizes novel specifications and a Solver that produces verified solutions, anchored by three mechanisms: a two-level group-relative update coupling Proposer advantages across specifications with Solver advantages across solution attempts; iterative self-distilled SFT projecting the base model onto its valid-output manifold before RL; and a UCB-guided Curriculum DAG whose policy-induced problem set can provably expand under self-composition. Without these stabilizers, sparse verifier feedback drives Proposer collapse even under MLRL-aligned rewards; with them, ANCORA bootstraps a verifiable curriculum from curated seeds. Instantiated in Verus, ANCORA lifts Dafny2Verus pass@1 from a 26.6% SFT baseline to 81.5% in test-time training (TTT, 0-shot), outperforming PSV self-play (1-shot) by 15.8 points; in a transfer setting, training from Dafny2Verus seeds yields 36.2% and 17.2% pass@1 on MBPP and HumanEval.
Machine Learning.comment: v3: Added a prompt-matched comparison with PSV, data-provenance audits, and a limitations section; corrected transcription errors in pass@5/10 values of Table 3; updated abstract; reformatted for journal submission

Machine Learning.title: QT-Net: Rethinking Evaluation of AI Models in Atomic Chemical Space
Machine Learning.summary: Atomic properties such as partial charges or multipoles encode chemically meaningful information that can inform downstream molecular property prediction, but their evaluation as machine learning targets has been complicated by the absence of a principled out-of-distribution evaluation protocol at the atomic level. In this work, we propose a held-out evaluation protocol that clusters atomic environments by SOAP descriptors and computes metrics accounting only for cluster labels unseen during training. Following this procedure, we use 5$\times$5 cross-validation and Tukey's HSD to run a statistically rigorous comparison of E(3)-equivariant against non-equivariant, rotationally augmented models for predicting electron populations and multipoles of H, C, N, and O atoms. Building on our results, we introduce the Quantum Topological Neural Network (QT-Net), a rotationally augmented, non-equivariant graph neural network. We show that QT-Net can be used to infer properties of atoms in molecules from QM9 outside our training set, and that the atomic environments seen during training strongly affect the performance of molecular property prediction tasks. To further validate the framework, molecular dipole moments computed from QT-Net's per-atom outputs recover the ground-truth values reported in QM9. We release all code and data, including a JAX implementation of QT-Net.

Machine Learning.title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery
Machine Learning.summary: Bayesian optimization is widely used in active learning loops for materials science. Gaussian processes serve as the de-facto surrogate model family, but require task-dependent kernel choices and can lack the modeling capacity for complex relationships. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have recently emerged as the state-of-the-art for predictive tasks on structured data, without requiring bespoke kernels or hyperparameter tuning. We evaluate two TFMs, TabPFN and TabICL, as out-of-the-box surrogate models on two standard materials science benchmarks, comparing against a large field of baselines encompassing Gaussian processes, random forests, and CatBoost. Our findings indicate that TFMs are highly competitive surrogate models across the two benchmarks, without task-specific training for active learning or GP kernel selection. Our results motivate developing TFMs further as surrogates for active learning in materials discovery.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at the AI4Mat Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. 19 pages, 12 figures, 5 tables. Code: https://github.com/PriorLabs/matsci-bo-bench

Machine Learning.title: Conformalized Super Learner
Machine Learning.summary: The Super Learner (SL) is a widely used ensemble method that combines point predictions from a library of learners based on their predictive performance. Interval predictions are of considerable practical interest because they allow uncertainty in predictions produced by an individual learner or an ensemble to be quantified. Several methods have been proposed for constructing interval predictions based on the SL, however, these approaches are typically justified using asymptotic arguments or rely on computationally intensive procedures such as the bootstrap. Conformal prediction (CP) is a machine learning framework for constructing prediction intervals with finite-sample and asymptotic coverage guarantees under mild conditions. We propose coupling CP with the SL through a natural construction that mirrors the original SL framework, using individual learner weights and combining learner-specific conformal prediction sets via a weighted majority vote. We characterize the properties of the resulting SL-based prediction intervals for continuous outcomes. We cover settings under exchangeability, and data-generating mechanisms exhibiting heteroscedasticity, sparsity, and other forms of distributional heterogeneity. A comprehensive simulation study shows that the conformalized SL achieves valid finite-sample coverage with competitive performance relative to the true data-generating mechanism. We present an application of this methodology to predict creatinine levels using socio-demographic, biometric, and laboratory measurements. This example demonstrates the benefits of an ensemble with carefully selected learners designed to capture key aspects of complex regression functions, including non-linear effects, interactions, sparsity, heteroscedasticity, and robustness to outliers.
Machine Learning.comment: R codes and data can be found at: https://github.com/ZWU-001/CSL

Machine Learning.title: Transformers converge to invariant algorithmic cores
Machine Learning.summary: Training selects for behavior, not circuitry: many weight configurations can implement the same function. Studying any single trained neural network thus risks describing accidents of one training run rather than the computation itself. This work shifts focus from what transformers happen to do to what they must do by extracting algorithmic cores, compact subspaces that are necessary and sufficient for a task and that recur across independently trained models. Here, Algorithmic Core Extraction (ACE) is introduced to isolate these subspaces, causally validate them, and recover the algorithms they implement, from synthetic tasks to large pretrained models. Markov-chain transformers embed 3D cores in nearly orthogonal subspaces yet recover identical transition spectra. Modular-addition transformers form compact cyclic cores at grokking that later inflate under continued regularization, redundantly distributing the same computation across many functionally equivalent modes. This functional redundancy accelerates the transition from memorization to generalization, yielding an inverse scaling law for grokking time. In six language models spanning two orders of magnitude in scale (GPT-2 Small/Medium/Large, LLaMA-3.1, Gemma-2, and Qwen2.5), subject-verb agreement is governed by a single, steerable axis that aligns across architectures. Flipping this axis inverts grammatical number throughout open-ended generation. For indirect object identification, a multi-step task, the same six models route computation through compact multi-dimensional cores at two sites, linked by a linear operator that transfers across model families. Together these results suggest that beneath the apparent complexity of trained transformers lies a simpler, shared computational structure, and that targeting invariants rather than parameterizations may offer a more tractable path to mechanistic understanding and control.

Machine Learning.title: Why Transformers Struggle with Distribution-Independent In-Context Learning
Machine Learning.summary: With in-context learning (ICL), transformer models adapt to new tasks from illustrative examples at inference time without updating their parameters. A common interpretation is that transformers implement implicit learning algorithms in their forward pass. We test this interpretation and ICL capability under distribution shift in noiseless polynomial regression, where the context uniquely determines the target function. Models that are near-perfect in distribution exhibit sharp performance degradation under shifts in the input or target-function distribution. This behavior persists across polynomial degrees and multiple training interventions, and in higher-dimensional nonlinear regression. We identify two architectural mechanisms that explain this breakdown: output saturation at finite boundary values linked to final normalization, and attention concentration on a small subset of the context, which can limit context-dependent adaptation required for ICL. Controlled experiments, architectural ablations, targeted interventions, and theoretical analysis provide strong evidence for both mechanisms and their consequence: strong in-distribution ICL does not imply distribution-independent ICL, which calls for caution when using ICL instead of explicit retraining or adaptation under distribution shift.
Machine Learning.comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

Machine Learning.title: Learning to Select Sparse Linear Solvers with Convolutional Neural Networks
Machine Learning.summary: We investigate convolutional-neural-network (CNN) based automatic solver selection for sparse linear systems, a problem of practical importance where solver performance varies dramatically with matrix sparsity structure. A CNN is trained to regress log timing ratios between candidate solvers using spy plot images of matrix nonzero structure as input, achieving strong prediction accuracy on both held-out SuiteSparse matrices and real-world matrices from high-performance simulation codes.

Machine Learning.title: Generative sequence modeling for infinite memory processes via predictive states
Machine Learning.summary: We consider estimating the one-step-ahead conditional distribution of a multivariate stochastic process. Many existing approaches rely on assumptions such as finite-range memory, sparsity, or additivity, which can be poorly suited to processes with long-range nonlinear interactions. However, without such structural assumptions, nonparametric estimation is challenging due to the curse of dimensionality. To address this challenge, we introduce a new estimator based on learning representations of the \emph{predictive states} of a stochastic process. We show that the statistical complexity of the estimation problem is determined by the dimension of this predictive state representation. Furthermore, we show that a $p$-dimensional predictive state space can be represented in a $2p+1$-dimensional feature space. Our results imply that faster convergence rates are achievable when the predictive state space is lower-dimensional, i.e., when the past history can be compressed into a lower-dimensional statistic that is sufficient for predicting the future. We establish theoretical convergence rate guarantees for an instantiation of our method based on deep neural network estimators. We implement our method in PyTorch and evaluate its performance on processes with infinite-range memory.

Machine Learning.title: Mitigating Global Feature Collapse in Graph ODEs via Hysteretic Topology Evolution
Machine Learning.summary: Graph neural ordinary differential equations provide continuous-time propagation on graphs, but their long-time behavior is largely determined by the asymptotic structure of the mixing operator. We show that diffusion-style Graph ODEs with positive irreducible mixing face a \emph{monostability trap}, where node features converge to a rank-one consensus subspace.
